\title{Stated or Sampled? Post-Training Narrows the Differential a Language Model Samples,\\Not the Single List It States}
\author{Jairam Hathwar\\University of Washington}
\date{Draft, \today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A language model's differential diagnosis can be read from the list it states in one answer or from the spread of its answers over repeated samples, the readout behind pass@$k$, self-consistency and sampling-based uncertainty. We compare the two readouts across base and post-trained versions of open 7--72B models from three families (Qwen, OLMo and Mistral) on DDXPlus, whose synthetic patients carry a reference differential, and on 897 published case reports.
First, direct-answer post-training collapses the sampled differential: post-trained models give 1.3--2.4 distinct answers per 32 samples, against 3.0--4.9, and with each model prompted at its best they lose 12--30 points of pass@32 (6--18 after correcting for chance, significant in five of seven pairs).
Second, one stated list keeps its coverage. Post-trained lists vary less from call to call, but zero-shot one list contains the true diagnosis more often for every Qwen model (robustly across prompts for the 7--8B ones), and on the case reports it covers as many of the alternatives the reports' authors considered as before (equivalent within 5 points), while the samples cover 8--14 points fewer for the Qwen models.
Third, tools that read the differential from samples lose value: on DDXPlus majority voting stops helping and agreement between samples weakens as an error signal, and once base models get the same worked examples and both decode greedily, post-training's first-answer gain is no longer significant in four of six pairs, and it is significantly lower in two when the base model's examples carry no reference list.
Drawing answers from the stated list restores the zero-shot base model's pass@32 for all but the OLMo~3 7B models. Studies of diagnostic breadth should report which readout they use, and systems that need several candidates should draw them from the stated list.
\end{abstract}

%=====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
Clinicians reason over a differential diagnosis, a ranked set of conditions consistent with the presentation, and the conditions they keep in view determine which tests are ordered and which dangerous possibilities are ruled out.
Language-model evaluations in medicine nonetheless score a single answer: multiple-choice accuracy, top-1 diagnosis, or at most pass@$k$ for a small $k$.
Post-training, whether general instruction tuning and RLHF or domain-specific medical reinforcement learning and distillation, is reported to improve these scores~\citep{chen2024huatuogpto1,liu2025alphamed,huang2025m1}.

A model's differential can be read in two ways: from the ranked list it states in one answer, or from the distribution of its answers over repeated samples.
Much current practice uses the second. Pass@$k$, self-consistency voting~\citep{wang2023selfconsistency} and sampling-based uncertainty such as semantic entropy~\citep{farquhar2024semanticentropy} all draw on repeated samples, and so does the evidence that reinforcement learning sharpens models, which win at $\passk{1}$ while their base models solve more problems given many samples~\citep{yue2025rlboundary,wu2025invisibleleash,oh2026sharpeningtax}.
The two readouts agree for a model that samples from the distribution it states. Work outside medicine suggests that aligned models do not. They can verbalize distributions they fail to sample from~\citep{meister2025distributional,zhang2025verbalized}, their verbalized confidence is better calibrated than their token probabilities~\citep{tian2023justask}, and their samples can homogenize enough to defeat sampling-based uncertainty~\citep{liu2026alignmenttax}.
\citet{jang2026cannotsample} show this directly for survey-response distributions: instruction-tuned models sample worse than their own base models, more so at each post-training stage, while still describing the target accurately in a single call. We measure what this means for differential diagnosis, where a reference differential and a true diagnosis are available for every case. This is a replication and extension of that work in a clinical setting, not a new phenomenon; one aligned answer can also cover what many base-model samples spread out~\citep{lake2025overton}.

The design that holds the pretrained model fixed and varies only the post-training:
(i) two base/instruct pairs, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B, which isolate general post-training;
(ii) three public medical models fine-tuned from the same parent, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: AlphaMed (rule-based RL), HuatuoGPT-o1 (SFT then PPO), and m1 (SFT distillation), plus AlphaMed's companion checkpoint trained from the base model;
(iii) every released stage of OLMo~3 7B~\citep{olmo2025olmo3}, from one base model through SFT, DPO and RL, plus a checkpoint trained with RL directly from the base;
(iv) at 32B, Qwen2.5-32B with its Instruct model and every released stage of OLMo~3.1 32B, and, added later, Qwen2.5-72B with its Instruct model.
We draw 32 samples per case. On DDXPlus~\citep{fansi2022ddxplus}, which ships a reference differential for every synthetic patient, we score both readouts against that reference; on rare-disease cases from Phenopacket Store~\citep{danis2025phenopacketstore} we score accuracy and stated confidence.

\paragraph{Findings.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Post-training collapses the sampled differential.} In both Qwen families at 7--8B the post-trained model is far better on its first answer (+13 to +27 points) but its pass@$k$ curve crosses the base model's at $k{\approx}4$--8, and at $k{=}32$ the base model leads by 10--15 points; at 32B the lead is smaller (4.0--4.9 points), though it grows to 15--19 points when every model sees three worked examples (\S\ref{sec:fewshot}); a Qwen2.5-72B pair, added later, repeats this ($-2.4$, n.s., zero-shot; $-12.3$ with worked examples) and still halves the distinct answers (\S\ref{sec:big32}). A third family, Mistral-7B prompted with worked examples, shows the same crossing, also with example lists from another model instead of the reference, whereas Qwen3-8B with its thinking mode on beats its base model at $k{=}32$ (\S\ref{sec:mistral}, \S\ref{sec:thinking}, \S\ref{sec:controls}). A hotter post-trained model is not a base model: along a temperature frontier with worked examples, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct and both 32B post-trained models reach less pass@32 than their base models at the same pass@1 (by 6.6--32 points; 4.5, n.s., for OLMo~3.1 32B at $T{=}1.3$) (at 32B the base model at $T{=}0.4$ beats its post-trained model on both readouts at every temperature), Qwen3-8B trades pass@32 for pass@1 at every temperature, and only Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct reaches its base model's frontier (\S\ref{sec:decoding}). Much of the first-answer gain is prompt format: with the same worked examples the sampled pass@1 gain falls to 1.6--5.2 points in four of six pairs, and decoded greedily, post-training raises top-1 significantly only for Qwen3-8B and Mistral, lowers it for Qwen2.5-32B and OLMo~3 7B under two of the three pairings, and is equivalent to the base model within 5 points in no pair (\S\ref{sec:fewshot}, \S\ref{sec:decoding}). Post-trained models give 1.3--2.6 distinct top answers per 32 samples, against 3.0--8.3, also when asked for one diagnosis per call instead of a list (\S\ref{sec:robust}), and can't-miss conditions drop out of their samples (\S\ref{sec:general}, \S\ref{sec:collapse}, \S\ref{sec:big32}). Which stage narrows the samples most depends on the recipe: the RL stage applied after SFT and DPO in OLMo~3 7B (19 points of $\passk{32}$), SFT in OLMo~3.1 32B (12 points), where the RL stage costs only 3 (\S\ref{sec:stages}).
\item \textbf{One stated list keeps its coverage; lists vary less across calls.} Within one call a post-trained list names as many conditions as a base-model list but more of the reference; across 32 calls the union of post-trained lists names 4.6--10 fewer conditions, though still covering more than twice the reference mass of the same model's samples; with sets of three, the most frequent sampled answers beat one list's top three for every base model, but the list wins for every post-trained Qwen model, so the list's advantage is not its length (\S\ref{sec:breadth}). A single stated list from the post-trained Qwen models at 7--32B is closer to the reference differential than the base model's (total-variation distance $-0.04$ to $-0.09$), covers 6--11 points more of its mass, and names severe conditions 9--14 points more often on average, while their samples move away from the reference. The same holds for OLMo~3.1 32B in TV and reference mass. A post-trained list tracks its own base model's averaged list for the same patient and barely changes between calls, so post-trained lists stay close to the base model's view (for the stronger models; Table~\ref{tab:packstrict}) and vary far less between calls; zero-shot, the post-trained Qwen lists contain the true pathology among their top five 12--16 points more often at $T{=}0.7$ (up to 24 at $T{=}1$) and allocate probability among named conditions more like the reference, but five averaged base-model lists get about as close (\S\ref{sec:aggregate}). Severe conditions are named more often on average, but specific ones, most often acute pulmonary edema, are lost (\S\ref{sec:statedchecks}). The gain survives restricting to complete lists, removing the true pathology, stratifying by top-1 correctness and correcting for each readout's floor (\S\ref{sec:statedchecks}). OLMo~3 7B's five-item lists do not improve, but its stated distribution does when asked for a probability on every condition (\S\ref{sec:stated}, \S\ref{sec:fullprompt}).
\item \textbf{Sampling-based methods lose their value; which signal to trust is model-dependent but cheap to check.} Majority voting over 32 samples gains base models 3--8 points at $T{=}0.7$ and the general post-trained models at most 1.9; models that reason before answering still gain 4--5. For post-trained Qwen models, the top three of one stated list beats the three most frequent of 32 sampled answers by 6--14 points. Agreement between samples becomes a weaker error signal in every family; the stated probability overtakes it for Qwen3-8B (and, not significantly, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct) but not for the other three general post-trained models. With five-sample agreement, averaging the two signals' ranks, with no labels, beats either signal for post-trained models (held-out AUROC 0.746 against 0.695 for agreement and 0.671 for the stated probability); a logistic model fitted on 100 labeled cases adds little (0.753). Qwen3-8B's thinking mode returns to the base-model pattern (\S\ref{sec:thinking}). Neither readout tracks how ambiguous a case truly is (\S\ref{sec:consequences}, \S\ref{sec:audit}).
\item \textbf{On real rare-disease cases the shifts replicate, though the top-three comparison does not flip.} Voting gains fall from 3.1--4.6 points for base models to 0.4--1.5 after post-training, and agreement weakens as an error signal until it ties the stated probability; 32 samples still beat one list (\S\ref{sec:phenoreadouts}).
\item \textbf{On published case reports the split holds, with or without a judge.} After post-training the 32 samples cover fewer of the alternatives the reports' authors considered, while one stated list covers them as before and names the final diagnosis more often; with a closed list of ten candidates graded by name, all four pairs show the split (\S\ref{sec:medcase}, \S\ref{sec:closedcase}).
\item \textbf{The lost breadth is recoverable from the stated list.} Drawing answers from the stated list restores pass@32 for every model except OLMo~3 7B's post-trained checkpoints, and given a random number, four of five post-trained models can do the drawing themselves, at a cost in first-answer accuracy for the 32B models; Qwen3-8B's picks stay narrow (\S\ref{sec:seeded}). The stated-list result also holds when the model chooses its list's length (\S\ref{sec:freelen}).
\item \textbf{Medical post-training adds accuracy, not breadth, and raises overconfidence on rare disease.} AlphaMed improves on its parent at every $k$ without widening its sampled differential; its companion checkpoint trained from the base model keeps most of the base model's diversity (\S\ref{sec:medical}). With accuracy near 2\%, medical RL raises stated confidence from 0.51 to 0.67--0.71, and every OLMo stage states 0.73--0.84 at about 1\% accuracy (\S\ref{sec:rare}).
\item \textbf{RL from the base model need not collapse the samples.} GRPO from Qwen3-8B-Base nearly matches the official post-trained model's top-1 accuracy while keeping more than twice its sampled diversity, and a group-level reward narrows the samples less than standard RLVR at equal accuracy (\S\ref{sec:training}).
\end{enumerate}

%=====================================================================
\section{Related work}
\paragraph{What RL does to a model's output distribution.}
\citet{yue2025rlboundary} find that RL with verifiable rewards improves $\passk{1}$ on math and code while base models win at large $k$.
\citet{wu2025invisibleleash} argue that RLVR mostly reweights solutions already in the base model's support.
\citet{oh2026sharpeningtax} document a ``sharpening tax'' across 14 base/post-trained pairs on agentic benchmarks.
In contrast, \citet{cheng2025guru} report that RL expands the boundary on domains under-represented in pretraining.
In medicine, the only pass@$k$ analysis we know of studies vision-language models and finds that RL mainly sharpens~\citep{jeddi2026medvlmrl}.
All of these measure the sampled distribution; we also measure the stated one.

\paragraph{Diversity loss from alignment.}
Instruction tuning and RLHF reduce output diversity~\citep{kirk2024rlhfdiversity,west2025basemodels,murthy2025onefish}, a loss that grows with scale for SFT~\citep{springer2026annotations}. Related work explains this as typicality bias in preference data~\citep{zhang2025verbalized} and documents cross-model homogeneity~\citep{jiang2025hivemind}.
\citet{zhang2025verbalized} also track diversity across the SFT, DPO and RLVR checkpoints of Tülu~3 on creative writing; we do the same for OLMo~3 against a clinical reference distribution.

\paragraph{Stated versus sampled distributions.}
\citet{meister2025distributional} find that language models asked to verbalize a group's opinion distribution match it better than their samples or log-probabilities do, and that they ``struggle to sample from their own distribution''; they study instruct and API models on opinion surveys, which have no correct answer.
Verbalized sampling~\citep{zhang2025verbalized} prompts aligned models to state a distribution over candidate responses and recovers part of the diversity lost in post-training.
\citet{tian2023justask} show that RLHF models' verbalized confidence is better calibrated than their token probabilities.
\citet{liu2026alignmenttax} report that aligned models' samples often fall into a single semantic cluster, leaving sampling-based uncertainty~\citep{kuhn2023semantic,farquhar2024semanticentropy} without signal on those questions; in a base/SFT/DPO stage ablation the collapse appears at DPO.
Closest to our question, \citet{jang2026cannotsample} show on synthetic and survey targets that instruction-tuned models sample worse than their own base models in every family they compare, that the gap grows at each OLMo-2 post-training stage, and that the same models describe the target accurately in one call. Verbalized-confidence studies reach mixed conclusions: sample consistency usually discriminates better than verbalized confidence~\citep{xiong2024express}, including for medical diagnosis~\citep{savage2025uncertainty}.
Our stated readout is the verbalized top-$k$ elicitation of \citet{tian2023justask}, and hybrids of consistency and verbalized confidence usually beat either~\citep{xiong2024express,lyu2024consistency,ren2026medconf}. We add a clinical task with a reference differential and a true diagnosis, two pipelines at 7--32B, and the consequences for aggregation and uncertainty.

\paragraph{Medical reasoning models and calibration.}
Medical post-training recipes include verifier-guided SFT and PPO~\citep{chen2024huatuogpto1}, minimalist rule-based RL~\citep{liu2025alphamed}, and test-time-scaling distillation~\citep{huang2025m1}.
Reward models and RL tend to favor confident answers~\citep{leng2025taming,damani2025rlcr}, and reasoning models are often overconfident~\citep{mei2025reasoninguncertainty}.
LLMs have been evaluated as differential-diagnosis aids on clinicopathological cases~\citep{kanjee2023jama,mcduff2025ddx} and in conversation~\citep{tu2025amie}, and base models have been excluded from clinical evaluations for failing to follow instructions~\citep{hager2024clinical}, the format problem our worked examples address. We show that this overconfidence appears in public medical descendants of one parent, on rare disease.

\paragraph{Differential diagnosis benchmarks and distributional RL.}
DDXPlus~\citep{fansi2022ddxplus} was introduced for automatic diagnosis systems trained on differentials~\citep{fansi2022casande}. Recent LLM evaluations on it score hierarchical top-$k$ accuracy~\citep{h-ddx2025} or interactive diagnosis~\citep{rose2025meddxagent}; the dataset's own metrics compare predicted and reference differentials as sets.
\citet{puri2026beyondmode} train models with GRPO to output several answers per forward pass, rewarding coverage of a gold \emph{set} and set-level calibration, and evaluate on DDXPlus.
We instead compare stated and sampled differentials against the reference \emph{distribution} across public post-trained model families.
Our group-level reward operates on the distribution of independently sampled answers (\S\ref{sec:training}).

%=====================================================================
\section{Experimental setup}\label{sec:setup}
\paragraph{Tasks.}
\textbf{DDXPlus}~\citep{fansi2022ddxplus}: synthetic patients produced by a rule-based medical knowledge base. Each patient has a true pathology and a reference differential, a probability distribution over the 49 conditions.
We use 980 test patients, 20 per condition. Each patient's coded symptoms and history are rendered as a short vignette; we fix known mistranslations in the English evidence descriptions.
The prompt lists all 49 conditions and asks for the five most likely, with probabilities, as JSON.
\textbf{Phenopacket Store}~\citep{danis2025phenopacketstore} (v0.1.27): published rare-disease cases annotated with HPO phenotypes and an OMIM diagnosis.
We use a disease-balanced set of 1,401 cases covering 749 diseases (at most two per disease). Each case is a vignette of present and absent phenotypes, and the model is asked for an open-ended differential.
Answers are graded by mapping names to Mondo; we credit an exact match, and separately a ``related'' match to a specific ancestor group or subtype.

\paragraph{Models.} Table~\ref{tab:models}. All checkpoints are public. For the medical models we verified the parent model from each released configuration.

\paragraph{Sampling.}
We draw $n{=}32$ samples per case with vLLM, at $T{=}0.7$, top-$p$ 0.95, and at $T{=}1.0$, top-$p$ 1.0 (sampling from the model's own distribution). All models use their chat template and the same prompt; OLMo-3-1025-7B ships without one, so it gets its SFT checkpoint's template.
Completions are capped at 4,096 tokens (8,192 for m1, whose long reasoning otherwise truncates), and generation stops at the end-of-turn token. The 32B models are sampled at $T{=}0.7$ only; the OLMo~3.1 32B SFT and DPO checkpoints, stored in float32, are run in bfloat16 like the other stages.
We take the last valid JSON list in each completion. Unparsable completions count as incorrect; this affects mainly base models, so base-model pass@$k$ is a lower bound at large $k$, while post-trained gains at small $k$ are partly format. \S\ref{sec:robust} reports format-controlled comparisons.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
\emph{pass@$k$}: the unbiased estimator of \citet{chen2021codex} on the top-1 answer of each sample.
\emph{Distinct} and \emph{entropy}: the number of distinct top-1 diagnoses across a case's 32 samples, and the entropy of their empirical distribution, averaged over cases.
On DDXPlus, \emph{TV}: total-variation distance between this empirical distribution and the reference differential.
\emph{Coverage@$k$}: the expected share of the reference differential's probability mass covered by the distinct top-1 answers in $k$ random samples.
\emph{Calibration}: expected calibration error (10 bins) of the stated top-1 probability against top-1 correctness.
These metrics describe the \emph{sampled} readout. \S\ref{sec:stated} defines the corresponding metrics for the \emph{stated} readout, the list in a single completion.
Differences come with 95\% paired-bootstrap intervals over cases (2,000 resamples) and are computed from unrounded values. We report many intervals without multiplicity correction; we treat a non-significant difference as ``no detectable change'', with the interval bounding its size, not as equivalence.

\section{Results}

\subsection{General post-training trades coverage for top-1 accuracy}\label{sec:general}
Table~\ref{tab:pairs} and Figure~\ref{fig:passk} compare each base model with its post-trained counterpart on DDXPlus.
In both families the post-trained model is much better on its first answer: +27.5 points for Qwen3 and +22.5 for Qwen2.5 at $T{=}1$ (intervals $[+20.3,+34.7]$ and $[+16.0,+29.2]$).
The advantage shrinks with $k$ and reverses: the curves cross at $k{\approx}4$--8, and at $k{=}32$ the base model leads by 14.6 points (Qwen3, $[+8.3,+21.5]$) and 10.3 points (Qwen2.5, $[+4.2,+17.3]$).
The pattern is the same at $T{=}0.7$ for Qwen3, crossing at $k{=}4$ with a base lead of 12.4 points at $k{=}32$ ($[+6.1,+19.8]$).
Unparsable base-model samples count as wrong, so these gaps are lower bounds.
Qwen2.5 at $T{=}0.7$ behaves the same way: +12.6 points at $k{=}1$ $[+6.7,+18.8]$ and a base lead of 9.7 at $k{=}32$ $[+4.1,+16.2]$.

\subsection{The sampled differential collapses, while top-1 calibration improves}\label{sec:collapse}
The gap at large $k$ reflects a collapsed \emph{sampled} differential.
Across 32 samples, the post-trained Qwen models name 1.3--2.7 distinct diagnoses per case, against 3.8--8.2 for their base models.
Their answer entropy is 0.11--0.49, against 0.78--1.58 for base models and 1.87 for the reference differential (Table~\ref{tab:pairs}).
Sampling at $T{=}1$ widens the base models' answers but barely changes the post-trained models' (Qwen3 entropy 0.11 at $T{=}0.7$, 0.18 at $T{=}1$), so the collapse lives in the model's own distribution rather than in the decoding settings.
As a result, post-trained models cover less of the reference differential: 0.24 vs.\ 0.41 of its probability mass at $k{=}32$ for Qwen3, and 0.29 vs.\ 0.42 for Qwen2.5.
Their top-1 calibration, however, is markedly better (ECE 0.06 vs.\ 0.20 and 0.14 vs.\ 0.29). This concerns verbalized confidence; alignment is known to worsen the calibration of token probabilities~\citep{openai2023gpt4,zhu2023calibration}, while verbalized confidence of RLHF models is better calibrated~\citep{tian2023justask}.
On every single-answer criterion (accuracy, small-$k$ pass@$k$, calibration), the post-trained model therefore looks strictly better, and the loss of breadth in its samples is invisible. Whether the breadth is lost from the model's stated differential as well is a separate question (\S\ref{sec:stated}).
\paragraph{Which diagnoses drop out?}
For each case and each condition that the reference differential weights at least 0.1, we ask whether the model names that condition as its top answer in at least one of its 32 samples. We call this \emph{considering} the condition.
We group the 49 conditions by DDXPlus severity (1 = most severe).
Post-training lowers consideration in every tier (Table~\ref{tab:severity}), and the severe tier (DDXPlus severity 1--2, the dataset's label rather than a clinical consensus list) is not spared. This metric needs a chance reference, though: a guesser that picks uniformly among the 49 conditions scores about 0.48 on it, and one that draws from the average reference differential 0.56--0.61, above every model, base models included. Considered@32 therefore measures the breadth of the sampled answers, not clinical judgement; we assess severe conditions on the stated list instead (\S\ref{sec:statedchecks}).
For the 17 severity-1--2 conditions (e.g.\ NSTEMI/STEMI, acute pulmonary edema, anaphylaxis, pulmonary embolism, unstable angina), consideration falls from 0.45 to 0.27 for Qwen3 and from 0.51 to 0.34 for Qwen2.5 at $T{=}1$. The differences are $-18.4$ $[-22.2,-14.6]$ and $-17.0$ $[-23.0,-11.5]$ points.
Some diagnoses disappear from the top answer almost entirely.
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct names unstable angina as its top answer in one of 107 eligible cases, where its base model does in 47\%. When unstable angina is the true pathology, $\passk{32}$ falls from 1.00 to 0.00. Stable angina (0.89 to 0.06) and myocarditis (0.41 to 0.00) follow the same pattern.
These conditions are not forgotten: they still appear lower in the listed differential (unstable angina in 50\% of eligible cases, against 95\% for the base model). The model ranks them but no longer commits to them.
At the same time, post-trained models concentrate on a few salient ``attractor'' diagnoses.
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct gives NSTEMI/STEMI as its top answer in 13.1\% of samples, against a reference rate of 4.4\% and 6.4\% for its base model. It also over-predicts pulmonary embolism (8.2\% vs.\ 3.2\%) and pneumonia (8.0\% vs.\ 2.4\%).
Chest-pain presentations thus collapse onto the most dangerous candidate. That raises its accuracy (NSTEMI $\passk{1}$ 0.99 vs.\ 0.44) at the cost of the alternatives. Ruling out acute coronary syndrome first is standard practice for chest pain, but these vignettes lack the ECG and biomarkers that would separate the coronary conditions, so we read this as a concentration of the samples, not as a clinical error.

\subsection{Robustness to prompt and output format}\label{sec:robust}
\paragraph{Prompt.} We repeat the Qwen3-8B pair with two other prompts (Table~\ref{tab:prompts}). \emph{Plain} drops the system prompt and rewords the instructions. \emph{CoT} asks the model to reason step by step before answering; Qwen3's thinking mode stays off in all runs.
The plain prompt reproduces the pattern: the post-trained model gains $+23.0$ $[+16.2,+30.3]$ points at $k{=}1$ and loses $-7.1$ $[-12.2,-2.4]$ at $k{=}32$ ($T{=}0.7$; at $T{=}1$, $+34.2$ and $-8.7$ $[-13.7,-4.0]$), with 1.3--1.5 distinct answers against 3.7--5.6.
Asking for reasoning changes the picture. With CoT, the post-trained model's $\passk{32}$ rises from 0.607 to 0.835: it leads the base model at every $k$ at $T{=}0.7$ ($+4.7$ $[+0.8,+9.1]$ at $k{=}32$) and ties it at $T{=}1$ ($0.0$ $[-3.3,+3.4]$).
Its samples remain far less diverse than the base model's (2.1--2.2 vs.\ 3.9--6.3 distinct answers), so reasoning recovers coverage at $k{=}32$ without restoring sampling diversity.
The coverage loss is therefore largest when the model answers directly, and reasoning at inference time mitigates it. This matches the medical models: the reasoning-trained descendants widen the differential (\S\ref{sec:medical}).

\paragraph{One diagnosis per call.} The sampled readout takes the first item of each five-item list, so the collapse could come from reading the top of a list. We therefore repeated the two 7--8B Qwen pairs at $T{=}0.7$ with a prompt that asks for the single most likely diagnosis, as a one-item JSON list, the format self-consistency and semantic entropy assume (Table~\ref{tab:single}). The collapse persists at about the same size: post-trained Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct give 1.18 and 1.43 distinct answers per 32 samples, against 3.49 and 3.84 for their base models (five-item prompt: 1.27 and 1.82 against 3.77 and 4.91), and lose 8.4 points of pass@32 each ($[-13.8,-3.4]$ and $[-13.9,-3.5]$; five-item prompt: 12.5 and 9.7) while gaining 21.7 and 15.3 at pass@1. Agreement among 31 further samples ranks the first answer's correctness less well after post-training (AUROC 0.824 $\rightarrow$ 0.607 and 0.822 $\rightarrow$ 0.683), and voting gains the base models 2.7 and 5.6 points and the post-trained models $-0.4$ and 1.4. Base models give invalid answers in 13.9\% and 9.4\% of samples. With one item per call the renormalized stated probability is always 1, so it carries no signal here.

\paragraph{Output format.} Base models more often give invalid answers: unparsable, or with a top answer outside the 49 conditions. This affects 12\% of Qwen3-8B-Base samples at $T{=}0.7$ and 25\% at $T{=}1$ (Qwen2.5-7B: 1\% and 21\%), against at most 0.3\% for the post-trained models.
Invalid samples count as wrong, which deflates the base model at large $k$ but inflates the post-trained model's gain at small $k$.
Among valid samples only, the post-trained models still gain $+12.0$ $[+5.2,+19.1]$ (Qwen3, $T{=}0.7$), $+18.7$ $[+12.1,+25.4]$ (Qwen3, $T{=}1$), $+12.2$ $[+6.3,+18.3]$ and $+16.8$ $[+10.9,+22.8]$ points (Qwen2.5) at $k{=}1$, so a quarter to a third of the raw gain at $T{=}1$ is format.
On the cases where every sample of both models is valid, the large-$k$ loss persists: $-15.2$ $[-25.5,-6.0]$ at $k{=}32$ for Qwen3 (105 cases) and $-10.2$ $[-17.1,-4.2]$ for Qwen2.5 (748 cases), both at $T{=}0.7$. (At $T{=}1$ almost no case has 32 valid base samples.) The reported large-$k$ losses are thus lower bounds.

\subsection{Which post-training stage narrows the differential?}\label{sec:stages}
The Qwen pairs compare a base model with the end of a post-training pipeline. OLMo~3~\citep{olmo2025olmo3} releases every stage of its 7B instruct pipeline from one base model: supervised fine-tuning, then DPO, then RL with verifiable rewards on math, code, instruction-following and chat prompts (the released OLMo-3-7B-Instruct). It also releases RL-Zero checkpoints trained with RL directly from the base; we use the general one, trained on chat prompts with an LM-judge reward. (The RL-Zero-Mix checkpoint does not load in our vLLM version.) Table~\ref{tab:stages} gives the results.

The coverage loss replicates in OLMo. At $T{=}0.7$, every post-trained stage is worse than the base at $k{=}32$: by $-14.6$ $[-20.9,-8.9]$ points after SFT, $-9.2$ $[-15.6,-3.1]$ after DPO, $-28.3$ $[-35.6,-21.2]$ after RLVR, and $-13.3$ $[-19.8,-7.3]$ for RL-Zero. Diversity falls at every stage of the pipeline, from 4.93 distinct answers for the base to 4.01 after SFT, 3.30 after DPO and 2.37 after RLVR.

Compared stage to stage, DPO recovers part of what SFT lost at large $k$ ($+5.4$ $[+0.3,+10.7]$ points at $k{=}32$, and $+10.3$ $[+6.2,+14.5]$ at $k{=}1$) while narrowing the differential further ($-0.71$ distinct answers).
The final RLVR stage is the largest single narrowing. Against the DPO model it loses $-19.1$ $[-24.8,-13.8]$ points at $k{=}32$, 0.92 distinct answers and 7.7 points of coverage@32, and it is also worse at $k{=}1$ ($-5.9$ $[-9.3,-2.8]$). It drops severe-tier Considered@32 to 0.25, a loss of $-16.1$ $[-21.1,-10.9]$ points relative to the base, against $-7.4$ for the DPO model. At $T{=}1$ the pattern is the same (RLVR vs.\ DPO: $-12.7$ $[-17.3,-8.2]$ at $k{=}32$).

RL applied directly to the base narrows the differential less. At $T{=}1$, RL-Zero shows no detectable loss of the base model's $\passk{32}$ ($-1.8$ $[-5.8,+2.1]$) and 6.28 of its 7.53 distinct answers, and it loses 4.0 $[0.9,7.1]$ points of severe-tier consideration, against 14.4 for the full instruct pipeline. At $T{=}0.7$ it still loses 13.3 points at $k{=}32$ ($[7.3,19.8]$), about as much as SFT.

The OLMo base model often breaks the output format: 40\% of its samples are invalid at $T{=}0.7$ and 47\% at $T{=}1$, while unparsable completions are 16--21\% for the SFT model and at most 2.0\% for the later stages. No case has 32 valid base samples, so the all-valid check of \S\ref{sec:robust} is not possible here. Among valid samples, the post-trained models' gains at $k{=}1$ are small ($-1.9$ to $+4.0$ points at $T{=}0.7$, $+1.3$ to $+8.1$ at $T{=}1$), so most of OLMo's raw gain at $k{=}1$ is format. Invalid samples count as misses and are excluded from distinct answers and entropy, so the base model's coverage and diversity are understated and the losses above are conservative.

Across these pipelines, then, the collapse of the sampled differential is not a necessary effect of RL. It accumulates over the instruction-tuning pipeline; in OLMo~3 7B its largest step is RL applied on top of SFT and DPO, but at 32B it is SFT (\S\ref{sec:big32}), so which stage narrows most depends on the recipe. RL applied directly to a base model (OLMo RL-Zero at $T{=}1$, AlphaMed's base-initialized checkpoint, and our GRPO runs in \S\ref{sec:training}) narrows the differential less, but not always: RL-Zero at $T{=}0.7$ loses about as much as SFT.
On Phenopacket Store the instruct pipeline also loses coverage: every stage trails the base model at $k{=}32$ ($-2.0$ $[-3.0,-1.0]$ points after SFT, $-1.5$ after DPO, $-1.4$ after RLVR; all significant), while RL-Zero does not ($-0.6$ $[-1.4,+0.2]$), from a base model at 4.5\% (\S\ref{sec:rare}).

\subsection{Replication at 32B and 72B}\label{sec:big32}
We repeat the DDXPlus comparisons at $T{=}0.7$ with Qwen2.5-32B and its Instruct model, and with every released stage of OLMo~3.1 32B, whose base is OLMo-3-1125-32B; there is no 32B RL-Zero checkpoint (Table~\ref{tab:big32}).
The sampled differential collapses at 32B too, by about half as much. Post-training costs 4.9 $[-0.6,10.4]$ points at $\passk{32}$ for Qwen2.5-32B and 4.0 $[1.3,6.8]$ for OLMo~3.1 32B (neither survives the headline correction), halves the number of distinct answers (3.78 $\rightarrow$ 1.68 and 4.32 $\rightarrow$ 2.15), and lowers severe-tier consideration by 6.1 and 8.4 points. For Qwen the loss holds on the 421 cases where every base sample is valid ($-4.8$ $[-9.6,-0.2]$); the OLMo 32B base gives invalid answers on 27\% of samples. With few-shot prompts, which nearly remove invalid answers, both losses are three to five times larger (\S\ref{sec:fewshot}).
The stage attribution differs from 7B. In OLMo~3.1 32B the largest narrowing is SFT ($\passk{32}$ $-12.1$ $[-18.0,-7.0]$, distinct answers $-1.39$, severe tier $-11.9$); DPO recovers most of it ($+10.9$ against SFT), and the final RL step is small ($-2.8$ $[-5.4,-0.5]$ at $k{=}32$, $-0.14$ distinct answers). OLMo~3.1 32B and OLMo~3 7B were post-trained with different recipes, so the stage that narrows the samples most is a property of the pipeline, not of SFT, DPO or RL as such.
Under this prompt the stated readout improves in both 32B families (\S\ref{sec:stated}; with few-shot prompts only Qwen2.5-32B's does robustly, \S\ref{sec:fewshot}), and voting stops paying off: majority voting over 32 samples gains the base models 7.0 and 8.4 points and the Instruct models 1.9 and 0.9 (the latter n.s.).

\paragraph{Qwen2.5-72B.} We added Qwen2.5-72B and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct after the headline tests were fixed, on DDXPlus at $T{=}0.7$ only, zero-shot and with the worked examples of \S\ref{sec:fewshot} (bottom of Table~\ref{tab:big32}); each prompt's 14 headline metrics are Holm-corrected together, outside the 112 primary tests. Its base model answers the zero-shot prompt validly (0.2\% invalid samples), so the zero-shot comparison needs no format control. Zero-shot, post-training raises pass@1 by 12.2 points and leaves pass@32 unchanged ($-2.4$ $[-6.9,1.8]$; $+0.9$ after chance correction), but it still halves the distinct answers (3.01 $\rightarrow$ 1.38) and lowers Cov@32 by 0.051 and the severe-tier coverage of the samples by 9.0 points. One list improves as for the smaller Qwen models: recall@5 rises by 15.4 points (0.706 $\rightarrow$ 0.859), TV falls by 0.059 (the list closes 21\% of the gap between the patient-blind list and the reference's top five, against 10\% for the base list), and the list names 8.5 points more reference mass and 9.6 points more of the warranted severe conditions. With worked examples the base model reaches pass@32 0.880 and post-training costs 12.3 points (8.8 $[3.6,14.6]$ after chance correction; Table~\ref{tab:chance}), its pass@1 gain is no longer significant ($+3.7$), and one list still gains (recall@5 $+6.4$, TV $-0.046$). Voting gains the base model 4.2 points zero-shot and 6.7 with worked examples, and the Instruct model 0.0 and 0.1; agreement's AUROC falls from 0.824 to 0.719 zero-shot and from 0.872 to 0.648 with worked examples, and the Instruct model's stated probability is ahead of agreement in both (0.741 and 0.769; not tested). Drawing each zero-shot sample's answer from its own list gives pass@32 0.885, above the base model's 0.755 (breadth in Table~\ref{tab:breadth}). As from 7--8B to 32B, the zero-shot pass@32 loss shrinks with scale, but the collapse of the samples, the stated list's gain and the loss of value of voting and agreement remain at 72B.

\subsection{The stated differential does not collapse}\label{sec:stated}
Every completion also \emph{states} a differential: up to five conditions with probabilities. We read it directly.
For each valid sample we renormalize its stated probabilities over the conditions it names (uniform if the probabilities are missing or invalid) and compare this single list with the reference differential: its total-variation distance to the reference, the reference mass of the conditions it names, and, for each severe condition with reference probability at least 0.1, whether the list names it.
For the sampled readout we use the empirical distribution of top-1 answers over the valid samples and, for the same budget of five names, the reference mass covered by the distinct top answers of five random samples.
Two oracles bound what each format can achieve: the reference's own top five stated as a list, and as many draws from the reference as the model has valid samples (Table~\ref{tab:stated}, Figure~\ref{fig:stated}).

For the Qwen models the two readouts move in opposite directions under post-training.
In both families and at both temperatures, the post-trained model's single list is closer to the reference than the base model's (TV $-0.043$ to $-0.086$, all intervals exclude zero), covers more of its mass ($+6.1$ to $+10.8$ points), and names severe conditions more often ($+9.1$ to $+13.4$ points).
Its sampled top answers move farther from the reference ($+0.029$ to $+0.071$), and five of them cover less ($-1.9$ to $-6.0$ points).
Within each post-trained model the list beats its own samples by 0.04--0.09 in TV; within each base model the gap is about zero or favors the samples.
The CoT prompt keeps the list's advantage (TV $-0.042$, severe naming $+8.1$ points) and removes the loss in the samples ($+0.002$, n.s.).
This quantifies the observation of \S\ref{sec:collapse} that conditions dropping out of the top answer remain lower in the list.

At 32B the pattern holds in both families (Table~\ref{tab:big32}): the post-trained lists are closer to the reference (TV $-0.053$ for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, $-0.052$ and $-0.045$ for the OLMo~3.1 DPO and Instruct models) and cover 5.6--6.7 points more of it, while the samples move away ($+0.014$ to $+0.034$). Within every post-trained 32B model the list beats its own samples by 0.04--0.09 in TV, against about zero for both base models.
OLMo~3 7B is the exception with the five-item prompt. Its DPO and Instruct models' lists are no closer to the reference than the base model's (TV $+0.000$ and $+0.028$ at $T{=}0.7$; $-0.026$ and $-0.005$ at $T{=}1$) and cover at most 5 points more of it; only the naming of severe conditions improves ($+6.1$ to $+12.8$ points). Asked for a probability on every condition, its Instruct model's stated distribution is closer to the reference than the base model's ($-0.032$ $[-0.038,-0.027]$; \S\ref{sec:fullprompt}), so the exception is specific to the short list. RL-Zero's lists improve slightly (TV $-0.020$ and $-0.039$).
The medical descendants change little relative to their parent (TV $-0.012$ for AlphaMed, $-0.014$ for HuatuoGPT-o1, $+0.017$ for m1).
In absolute terms every model is far from the reference: a single list covers 0.22--0.41 of the reference mass, against 0.74 for the reference's own top five.

\paragraph{Few-shot prompting.}With three worked examples in every prompt, the Qwen gains persist or grow (TV $-0.057$ to $-0.087$; $-0.055$ to $-0.073$ without the true pathology), but OLMo~3.1 32B's list keeps only its higher reference mass ($+0.047$), with TV, TV without the true pathology and DDF1 no longer significant (Appendix~\ref{sec:fewshot}). Averaging calls narrows the gap: the mean of five base-model lists is about as close to the reference as one post-trained list (Qwen3-8B 0.699 against 0.700); a post-trained list tracks its own base model's view of the patient and barely varies between calls (\S\ref{sec:aggregate}), and Qwen3-8B's thinking mode goes further, with one list beating five averaged base lists.

\subsection{Consequences for sampling-based methods}\label{sec:consequences}
We ask what the gap does to two common uses of repeated samples: aggregating them into an answer, and using their agreement as an uncertainty signal (Table~\ref{tab:consequences}). The single-call answer is the top answer of a model's first valid sample.

\paragraph{Aggregation.}
Majority voting over 32 samples (self-consistency;~\citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}) raises base models' accuracy by 3.4--5.2 points at $T{=}0.7$ and 10.4--14.2 at $T{=}1$.
For the general post-trained models it adds at most 0.8 points at $T{=}0.7$ (Qwen3-8B $+0.3$, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct $+0.8$, OLMo-3-Instruct $-0.2$; all n.s.) and 0.1--4.4 at $T{=}1$.
Models that reason before answering still benefit (HuatuoGPT-o1 $+4.8$, m1 $+3.8$, Qwen3-8B with the CoT prompt $+4.5$).
Averaging the stated lists instead of voting changes accuracy by at most about 2 points for any model.
For a top-three differential, the stated list is the better source after post-training. For Qwen3-8B, the top three of one list contains the true pathology $13.7$ $[+11.4,+15.9]$ points more often than the three most frequent answers in 32 samples ($T{=}1$: $+10.0$), and for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct $7.3$ $[+5.3,+9.6]$ points more often ($T{=}1$: $+2.0$, n.s.).
For every base model the 32 samples win, by 7.3--13.6 points at $T{=}0.7$. OLMo-3-Instruct is in between ($+1.9$, n.s.; $T{=}1$: $-4.7$). Collapsed samples often offer fewer than three answers, though: matched for size, the post-trained list is no better than its samples ($-0.5$ to $-5.2$ points), while base models' samples still win by 8.5--14.6 (\S\ref{sec:further}).

\paragraph{Uncertainty.}
We score how well each signal ranks the correctness of the single-call answer (AUROC). The stated probability of that answer needs no extra calls; \emph{agreement}, the share of the model's other samples with the same top answer, uses 4 or 31 more.
For base models agreement is far better: 0.80--0.81 with 31 extra samples, against 0.54--0.60 for their nearly uninformative stated probability.
Post-training weakens agreement in every family (Qwen3 0.810 $\rightarrow$ 0.655, Qwen2.5 0.811 $\rightarrow$ 0.702, OLMo 0.802 $\rightarrow$ 0.731), consistent with \citet{liu2026alignmenttax}, and moves the comparison toward the stated probability.
For Qwen3-8B (0.734) and OLMo-3-Instruct (0.796), the stated probability is better than agreement over 32 samples ($+0.079$ $[+0.046,+0.110]$ and $+0.064$ $[+0.027,+0.101]$); at $T{=}1$ the two are statistically tied.
For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (0.571 vs.\ 0.702) and all three medical models, agreement remains better.
These AUROCs are computed on each model's own answers, so they compare signals within a model, not models with each other.

\paragraph{Ambiguity.}
The reference differential also says how ambiguous each case is. We correlate each uncertainty signal with the entropy of the case's reference differential.
For every model and signal the Spearman correlation lies between $-0.10$ and $+0.14$, except AlphaMed's stated probability and stated entropy ($+0.30$ and $+0.32$).
How uncertain a model is about a case, by either readout, says almost nothing about how ambiguous the case is.

\paragraph{At 32B.}
The same shifts appear with smaller margins. Voting gains fall from 7.0 and 8.4 points for the base models to 1.9 and 0.9 (the latter n.s.) for the Instruct models, and agreement weakens as an error signal (Qwen 0.797 $\rightarrow$ 0.721, OLMo 0.831 $\rightarrow$ 0.772). For Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct the top three of one list beats the three most frequent of 32 sampled answers by 5.6 $[3.6,7.7]$ points, but its stated probability only ties agreement over 32 samples ($-0.011$, n.s.; it beats agreement over five, $+0.047$); for OLMo~3.1 32B Instruct agreement stays better ($-0.077$).

After post-training, then, repeated sampling adds little: voting no longer improves accuracy and agreement carries less signal, while one stated list carries as much of the differential or more. Where the crossover falls depends on the model, so neither readout can be assumed to be the informative one without checking.

\subsection{Robustness of the stated readout to elicitation}\label{sec:fullprompt}
The stated readout above uses a five-item list. We repeat the Qwen pairs and OLMo~3 7B's base and Instruct models at $T{=}0.7$ with a prompt that asks for a probability on every one of the 49 conditions, summing to one, and take each sample's top answer to be its highest-probability condition (Table~\ref{tab:fullprompt}).
The results match the short list for Qwen. After post-training the stated distribution is closer to the reference (TV $-0.052$ for Qwen3-8B, $-0.067$ for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $-0.032$ for OLMo-3-7B-Instruct) while the samples move away ($+0.012$ to $+0.038$); OLMo-3-7B-Instruct's full distribution moves closer although its five-item list does not.
Qwen3-8B's stated probability again beats agreement over 32 samples ($+0.069$ $[+0.013,+0.127]$), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's again does not ($-0.074$), and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct's ties it ($-0.010$; $+0.044$ against five samples). The top three of one full distribution beats the three most frequent of 32 sampled answers for Qwen3-8B ($+14.6$ points) and narrowly for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($+1.6$), but not for OLMo-3-7B-Instruct ($-9.5$).

\subsection{Breadth within one list and across calls}\label{sec:breadth}
A five-item list cannot get shorter, so breadth within one call and breadth across calls need separate measures (Table~\ref{tab:breadth}). Within one call, post-trained lists name as many conditions as base-model lists (4.9--5.0) and carry more of the reference: 5--9 points more of its probability and 7--13 points more of the conditions it weights at least 0.1 (the upper ends from the later Qwen2.5-72B pair), significant for every pair but OLMo~3 7B, whose lists do not change. Across 32 calls the stated readout narrows: because post-trained lists vary little, their union names 4.6--10.0 fewer conditions than the union of the base model's lists, covers 10--13 points less reference mass and 7--14 points fewer warranted conditions (all significant). The union of 32 post-trained lists still covers more than twice the reference mass of the same model's 32 sampled answers (0.47--0.59 against 0.20--0.28). Narrowing across calls therefore affects both readouts, but much less the stated one, and a single list loses nothing.

\paragraph{Sets of equal size.} A five-item list could beat the sampled answers simply because it names more conditions. Comparing sets of three, the top three of one list against the three most frequent of 32 sampled answers (zero-shot, $T{=}0.7$; Table~\ref{tab:consequences}), the samples contain the true pathology more often for every base model (by 7.3--13.6 points), while for every post-trained Qwen model the list does (by 5.6--13.7 points) and the OLMo Instruct models are about even ($+1.9$ and $-0.6$); for Qwen2.5-72B the values are $-7.4$ (base) and $+8.4$ (Instruct). Which readout covers more therefore reverses with post-training rather than following from the list's length; the base models' samples miss the true pathology while their first list names it for only 2.9--3.5\% of patients, against 7.2--19.9\% for the post-trained models (Qwen3-8B 19.9, Qwen2.5-7B 14.7, Qwen2.5-72B 14.1, OLMo~3 7B 13.1, Qwen2.5-32B 11.0, OLMo~3.1 32B 7.2).

\subsection{Free-length lists}\label{sec:freelen}
The stated readout uses five-item lists, so a narrower view could hide behind the fixed length. We repeated the three Qwen pairs at $T{=}0.7$ with a prompt that asks for every condition the model considers plausible, as many or as few as it judges appropriate (Table~\ref{tab:freelen}). Length moves both ways: Qwen3-8B's lists grow after post-training (7.0 to 9.9 conditions), while the Qwen2.5 instruct models write shorter lists than their base models (5.2 against 10.7, and 4.0 against 5.8), whose lists often run on until the token limit. Whatever their length, post-trained lists contain the true pathology more often (by 8.8--16.3 points) and are closer to the reference (TV $-0.047$ to $-0.072$). They name as much reference mass or more ($+14.9$, $-1.9$ n.s., $+2.8$ points) and, for both Qwen2.5 models, allocate it more like the reference (conditional TV $-0.144$ and $-0.078$; Qwen3-8B $+0.026$, n.s.\ after correction). The sampled answers collapse as under the standard prompt (2.5--2.9 fewer distinct answers). The fixed length therefore does not hide a narrower stated view.

\subsection{Ruling out format, accuracy and floor effects}\label{sec:statedchecks}
Table~\ref{tab:robust} tests simpler explanations of the stated-list result. For reference, one list's recall@5 rises after post-training by 13.6, 16.2 and 12.0 points for Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B at $T{=}0.7$ and by 21.9 and 24.0 for the 7--8B Qwen models at $T{=}1$, by 12.7 for OLMo~3.1 32B, and for OLMo~3 7B by 1.5 (n.s.) at $T{=}0.7$ and 10.0 at $T{=}1$ (condition-clustered intervals exclude zero except where marked).
\emph{Format.} The general models' post-trained lists and base-model lists at $T{=}0.7$ are nearly all complete (82--99\% name five on-list conditions with probabilities; Qwen base models at $T{=}1$, 61--62\%; the medical models, 61--80\%). Restricting to complete lists leaves the gaps unchanged (Qwen2.5-7B: 0.778 vs.\ 0.716).
\emph{Accuracy.} A more accurate model puts more stated mass on the true pathology, which the reference also favors. Within samples whose top answer is correct, and within those whose top answer is wrong, the post-trained Qwen list is still closer to the reference ($-0.013$ to $-0.041$ and $-0.030$ to $-0.090$ in TV across both temperatures; Table~\ref{tab:robust} shows $T{=}0.7$).
\emph{Floor.} One list can do no better than the reference's own top five, and a finite set of samples no better than as many draws from the reference. Measured as excess over these floors, post-training lowers the list's TV (Qwen3-8B 0.479 $\rightarrow$ 0.436) and raises the samples' (0.557 $\rightarrow$ 0.613).
\emph{True pathology removed.} With the true pathology removed from both list and reference and both renormalized, the post-trained Qwen and OLMo~3.1 32B lists are still closer to the reference ($-0.018$ to $-0.056$), and DDXPlus's set F1 against the reference's support improves by 0.040--0.083 (Table~\ref{tab:clustered}). TV, mass and DDF1 are not independent, since a list's TV is the reference mass it leaves out plus the mass it misallocates among the conditions it names, and the second term grows mechanically with the first. The conditional TV, between the list and the reference restricted to the named conditions and renormalized, removes this: it falls after post-training for every Qwen pair and OLMo~3.1 32B ($-0.025$ to $-0.078$, all surviving correction) and rises for OLMo~3 7B at $T{=}1$ ($+0.064$), so the Qwen lists both name better conditions and weight them more like the reference.
\emph{Patient-blind list.} A fixed list of the five conditions with the highest average reference probability scores TV 0.794, mass 0.238 and DDF1 0.272. Every model's list beats it in TV except OLMo~3 7B's and Qwen2.5-7B's base list at $T{=}1$; in DDF1 several base lists do not (Qwen2.5-7B 0.245, OLMo~3 7B 0.225), and the post-trained Qwen and OLMo~3.1 32B lists exceed it by 0.035--0.061.
\emph{Over-naming.} As a share of named conditions, post-trained lists name fewer that the reference gives less than 1\% (Qwen3-8B 0.59 $\rightarrow$ 0.55) and fewer unwarranted severe conditions (Qwen2.5-32B 0.80 $\rightarrow$ 0.73), but as a count per list the change is mixed: from 0.22 fewer unwarranted severe conditions (OLMo~3.1 32B) to 0.35 more (OLMo~3 7B).
\emph{Severe conditions one by one.} Table~\ref{tab:severetest} tests each of the 17 severe conditions, counting it wherever the reference gives it any weight. After Benjamini--Hochberg correction, 2--7 conditions per zero-shot pair are named significantly less often after post-training and 0--6 significantly more often, and no pair names more conditions less often than a random swap of base and post-trained lists would. With the warranted threshold at 0.01 or 0.05 instead of 0.1, post-trained lists still name more severe conditions in seven of eight zero-shot settings ($+2.5$ to $+8.1$ points; OLMo~3.1 32B n.s.). That count test is weak against an overall upward shift, so Table~\ref{tab:severetest} also gives the mean shift across the 17 conditions: it rises significantly in seven of eight zero-shot settings but falls with worked examples for Qwen2.5-32B ($-0.012$) and OLMo~3 7B ($-0.018$), and is flat for Mistral ($-0.009$, $p{=}0.05$). Significant losses include acute pulmonary edema (Qwen3-8B 0.75 $\rightarrow$ 0.61, Qwen2.5-32B 0.63 $\rightarrow$ 0.44, OLMo~3 7B 0.56 $\rightarrow$ 0.31, OLMo~3.1 32B 0.57 $\rightarrow$ 0.41), stable angina (Qwen2.5-7B 0.25 $\rightarrow$ 0.08), NSTEMI/STEMI (OLMo~3 7B 0.31 $\rightarrow$ 0.14, OLMo~3.1 32B 0.49 $\rightarrow$ 0.36) and myocarditis (Qwen2.5-32B 0.14 $\rightarrow$ 0.05); significant gains include pulmonary embolism (Qwen2.5-7B 0.29 $\rightarrow$ 0.56, OLMo~3 7B 0.20 $\rightarrow$ 0.65), NSTEMI/STEMI (Qwen2.5-7B 0.32 $\rightarrow$ 0.52) and unstable angina (Qwen3-8B 0.14 $\rightarrow$ 0.37). Among single stages, OLMo~3 7B's RLVR step and OLMo~3.1 32B's SFT and RLVR steps do name more conditions less often than chance (12--13 of 17, $p{=}0.03$--0.04).

\emph{Sampling from the list.} Replacing each sample's top answer with a draw from its own stated list raises $\passk{32}$ for every model but the OLMo~3 7B base (0.700 against 0.705). Compared like for like, post-trained lists reach higher than their base model's lists in five of seven comparisons (Qwen3-8B 0.812 vs.\ 0.787 at $T{=}0.7$, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct 0.883 vs.\ 0.856, OLMo~3.1 32B Instruct 0.847 vs.\ 0.840), but not for Qwen3-8B at $T{=}1$ (0.815 vs.\ 0.834) or OLMo~3 7B (0.574 vs.\ 0.700), and a uniform guesser reaches 0.48. Drawn pass@32 stays below the share of cases whose lists' union contains the true pathology (e.g.\ Qwen3-8B 0.812 against 0.847), so drawing realizes most, not all, of what the lists contain.
OLMo~3 7B remains the exception throughout: its Instruct list is closer to the reference when its top answer is correct but much farther when it is wrong.

\subsection{Can the model draw from its own list?}\label{sec:seeded}
Drawing each sample's top answer from its own stated list restores pass@32 for every model except the OLMo~3 7B post-trained checkpoints (\S\ref{sec:statedchecks}), but that draw happens outside the model. To test whether a post-trained model can do it itself, in the spirit of prompting for verbalized distributions~\citep{zhang2025verbalized}, we gave each of 32 calls its own random number $u$ (stratified over $[0,1]$) and asked the model to state its list as usual and then pick the condition at which the running total of its rescaled top-five probabilities first reaches $u$ (Table~\ref{tab:seeded}). Picks are almost always present and on the model's own list, but the rule is followed only partly: in 39--40\% of calls for the 7--8B Qwen models, 58\% and 65\% for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, and 84\% for OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct. Four of five models recover breadth: 1.1--4.3 more distinct answers and 7.2--26.8 more points of pass@32 than their ordinary samples, which leaves none of them significantly below its base model's pass@32 and OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct significantly above it ($+5.7$). Qwen3-8B follows the rule as often as Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct but rarely picks a lower-ranked condition when the rule calls for one: its picks are as narrow as its samples (1.25 distinct answers, against 5.96 if it followed the rule) and stay 15.7 points below its base model. Where recovery works best it costs first-answer accuracy: pass@1 falls by 20.3 points for both 32B models, as expected when answers are drawn in proportion to the list rather than taken from its top. The extra instruction leaves the stated lists unchanged (recall@5 within 0.02 and TV within 0.01 of the ordinary lists, except OLMo-3-7B-Instruct's, which improve), and agreement among the picks is no better an error signal than ordinary agreement for any model. Applying the rule ourselves to each call's list would give pass@32 of 0.70--0.89. Breadth is thus recoverable from the stated list, reliably when the drawing is done outside the model.

\subsection{Few-shot elicitation}\label{sec:fewshot}
The main analyses give every model the same zero-shot chat prompt, which base models were not trained to follow; they give invalid answers on up to 47\% of samples, which we count as wrong. We therefore re-ran the five final base/post-trained pairs at $T{=}0.7$ with three worked examples in the prompt: three fixed DDXPlus training patients with different true pathologies, each followed by the top five conditions of its reference differential, with probabilities, in the JSON format the instructions ask for. Base models see the instructions and examples as a plain document and complete the next one (generation stops at the end of the list); post-trained models see the same instructions and examples as earlier chat turns. Invalid samples fall below 0.5\% for every model (Table~\ref{tab:fewshot}).

The examples help base models most. Their pass@1 rises from 0.178 to 0.306 for OLMo-3-1025-7B, from 0.326 to 0.528 for OLMo-3-1125-32B and from 0.500 to 0.647 for Qwen2.5-32B, and their pass@32 reaches 0.76--0.90, while their stated lists barely change (TV 0.712--0.787, against 0.726--0.794 zero-shot). The losses in the samples therefore grow (Table~\ref{tab:fewshotdiff}): post-training costs 15.2--29.9 points of pass@32 in every pair, including both 32B pairs, whose zero-shot losses did not survive correction, and every post-trained model's Cov@32 (0.21--0.25) is below every base model's (0.33--0.45) and below a uniform guesser's.

For the three Qwen pairs the stated-list improvement persists and mostly grows: TV $-0.057$ to $-0.087$, $-0.055$ to $-0.073$ with the true pathology removed, and DDF1 $+0.051$ to $+0.081$, all surviving correction. OLMo~3 7B remains the exception (TV $+0.021$, n.s.; $+0.024$ without the true pathology). For OLMo~3.1 32B the improvement shrinks: the post-trained list still places more reference mass on the conditions it names ($+0.047$), but its TV ($-0.022$), TV without the true pathology ($-0.006$) and DDF1 ($+0.009$) no longer survive correction. At 32B the stated-list result is therefore robust for Qwen2.5-32B but depends on the prompt for OLMo~3.1 32B. Post-trained lists still name 5--10 of the 17 severe conditions less often than their base model's.

The consequences replicate in all five pairs. Majority voting over 32 samples gains base models 6.2--10.9 points and post-trained models 0.2--1.1. The three most frequent of 32 sampled answers beat the top three of one stated list by 8.2--22.0 points for base models, while for post-trained models the list is ahead by 0.2--16.7. Agreement with four more samples is the better error signal for every base model (AUROC 0.79--0.84, against 0.67--0.73 for the stated probability), and the stated probability for every post-trained model (0.69--0.77, against 0.56--0.68); against agreement across 31 samples the stated probability wins clearly only for Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($+0.108$ and $+0.130$, clustered) and ties for the others.
This check uses one temperature and one set of examples, and the examples show the reference's own lists, which may help every model match the reference.

\label{tab:fewshotdiff}

\subsection{Two further controls}\label{sec:controls}
\paragraph{Reference-free few-shot examples.} The examples of \S\ref{sec:fewshot} show each training patient's reference top five, and so also the target of the evaluation. We re-ran the six final pairs with the same three patients but with each example list replaced by Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct's own greedy answer (on-list, with the true pathology first for two patients and second for one). The conclusions do not change (Table~\ref{tab:refree}). Post-training costs 12.7--29.7 points of pass@32 in every pair. The stated list moves closer to the reference for the three Qwen pairs and, now clearly, for Mistral (TV $-0.053$ to $-0.077$; $-0.031$ to $-0.059$ with the true pathology removed), but not for OLMo~3 7B or OLMo~3.1 32B, and wherever the list improves its allocation among the named conditions also moves closer to the reference (conditional TV $-0.051$ to $-0.100$). Voting helps base models by 3.7--13.7 points and post-trained ones by at most 1.4; the top three of one list beats the three most frequent samples for every post-trained model; the stated probability beats agreement as an error signal for every post-trained model and agreement beats it for every base model; and no pair names more severe conditions less often than chance. Five of six base models score lower at $k{=}1$ than with reference-derived examples (OLMo-3-1125-32B 0.453 against 0.528).

\paragraph{Matched temperature.} Post-trained models are sharper than their base models at the same nominal temperature, so part of the narrowing could be colder effective sampling. We sampled Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $T{=}1.3$ and 1.6 (Table~\ref{tab:matcht}), and the two models differ. Qwen3-8B barely broadens: at $T{=}1.6$ it gives 1.92 distinct answers and reaches 0.684 at pass@32, still below its base model at $T{=}0.7$ (0.732) and at $T{=}1$ (0.789; $-10.5$ points, surviving correction); voting gains stay under 2 points, agreement stays weaker than for the base model, and its stated list does not change (TV 0.701). Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct does broaden: at $T{=}1.3$, with 2\% invalid answers, it gives 3.38 distinct answers, matches its base model's pass@32 at $T{=}0.7$ (0.704 against 0.695), gains 5.6 points from voting, and agreement is again the better error signal (0.794 against 0.602), at a cost of 4.2 points of pass@1; at $T{=}1.6$, 31\% of its answers are invalid. Its stated list stays closer to the reference than the base model's (0.722 against 0.779). For some models, then, much of the sampled narrowing is sharper sampling that a higher temperature undoes; the stated-list result is not.

\subsection{Greedy decoding, temperature frontier and a must-not-miss prompt}\label{sec:decoding}
\paragraph{Greedy single call.} Deployed systems often decode greedily. We compared one greedy answer per case under three prompt pairings (Table~\ref{tab:greedy}): both arms with the reference-derived worked examples of \S\ref{sec:fewshot} (\emph{same examples}); base models with the reference-free examples of Table~\ref{tab:refree} against zero-shot post-trained models, so that neither arm sees a reference list (\emph{reference-free base}); and reference-example base models against zero-shot post-trained models, the pairing we first ran. Under every pairing post-training significantly raises top-1 in at most two of six pairs. With the same examples these are Qwen3-8B ($+13.7$) and Mistral ($+10.8$); Qwen2.5-7B gains $+1.8$ and the other three lose 4.8--5.8 points, all n.s. With reference-free base models only Qwen3-8B gains ($+10.7$), while Qwen2.5-32B ($-8.0$) and OLMo~3 7B ($-14.5$) lose significantly. The example lists matter little to the base models (top-1 within 2.7 points, except OLMo~3.1 32B, 0.630 against 0.559) but raise five of the six post-trained models (Mistral 0.417 to 0.577, OLMo~3 7B 0.258 to 0.345; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct falls to 0.458). Under every pairing the two smaller Qwen models' lists contain the true pathology more often (recall@5 $+16.8$ to $+26.0$) and name more warranted severe conditions, every Qwen list is closer to the reference, and OLMo~3 7B's lists are farther. Together with the few-shot comparison, where the sampled pass@1 gain is already only 1.6--5.2 points in four of six pairs, much of post-training's advantage at one sampled call for the 7--8B Qwen models ($+12.6$ to $+27.5$ points at $T{=}0.7$ and 1, \S\ref{sec:collapse}) is therefore prompt format and the base model's sampling noise; Qwen3-8B and Mistral keep a real gain. These are not equivalence results: with the margin of 5 points fixed in advance, no pair's greedy top-1 is equivalent to its base model's under either pairing (TOST at the 5\% level), so the gain is no longer significant rather than shown to vanish.

\paragraph{Temperature frontier.} With worked examples and top-$p$ fixed at 1, we sampled the three 7--8B pairs at $T = 0.4$, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 (Table~\ref{tab:frontier}). Post-trained pass@1 barely moves with temperature (Qwen3-8B 0.60, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 0.43--0.46, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct 0.29--0.35), pass@32 rises (to 0.70, 0.66 and 0.74 at $T{=}1.3$), and the stated list barely changes (TV 0.68, 0.70 and 0.81--0.83), consistent with the concentration described by \citet{yang2026concentration}. Base models trade pass@1 (Qwen3-8B-Base 0.45 to 0.18) for pass@32, which peaks at $T{=}1$ or 1.3 (0.85--0.88), and 25--36\% of their answers are invalid at $T{=}1.3$. The frontiers differ by family. For Qwen3-8B the post-trained model is better at pass@1 and the base model at pass@32 at every temperature tested; for Qwen2.5-7B the curves meet (at pass@1 about 0.43, the base model at $T{=}0.4$ and the Instruct model at $T{=}1.3$ both reach pass@32 0.66); and for OLMo~3 7B the base model at $T{=}0.4$ beats its Instruct model at every temperature on both (0.368 and 0.803, against at best 0.345 and 0.737). Interpolating the base model's frontier at the Instruct model's pass@1, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct reaches 13.0--31.9 points less pass@32 at each temperature (condition-clustered intervals exclude zero); for Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct the post-trained pass@1 lies above every base point, so no matched comparison exists. We repeated the frontier for the two 32B pairs (Table~\ref{tab:frontier32}). There the base model at $T{=}0.4$ beats its post-trained model on both pass@1 and pass@32 at every temperature, and at the post-trained model's pass@1 the base frontier reaches 7.4--15.4 points more pass@32 for Qwen2.5-32B and 4.5--17.0 for OLMo~3.1 32B (intervals exclude zero except OLMo at $T{=}1.3$), although the zero-shot 32B losses do not survive correction (\S\ref{sec:big32}). Agreement becomes a better error signal for post-trained models as temperature rises (Qwen3-8B 0.57 to 0.68) but stays below the base models' (0.81--0.92).

\paragraph{Must-not-miss prompt.} The standard prompt asks for the most likely conditions. We asked the six post-trained models for the five most likely conditions and then up to three dangerous conditions to rule out (Table~\ref{tab:mnm}). Whole lists then name 0.44--0.58 of the severe conditions that the reference weights at least 0.1, 6--15 points more than with the standard prompt and 11--21 more than the base models' lists, and acute pulmonary edema is recovered for every model but Qwen3-8B (e.g. Qwen2.5-32B 0.44 $\rightarrow$ 0.63, OLMo~3 7B 0.31 $\rightarrow$ 0.58). The cost is 1.1--2.1 more unwarranted severe conditions per list, mostly pulmonary embolism, named in 88--100\% of eligible cases, and for Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Mistral a shorter most-likely part that contains the true pathology 5--10 points less often. Even when asked, no model names more than 0.58 of the warranted severe conditions.

\subsection{Must-not-miss conditions defined outside DDXPlus}\label{sec:extmnm}
The severity label used above is the dataset's own. We therefore re-ran every severe-condition analysis with two published sets of conditions that must not be missed, mapped onto DDXPlus's 49 (Table~\ref{tab:extmnm}): a harm-based set, the DDXPlus conditions among the 15 diseases that cause about half of serious misdiagnosis-related harms in the USA~\citep{newmantoker2024burden} (NSTEMI/STEMI, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia and pulmonary neoplasm, of which DDXPlus labels only the first two severe), and the life-threatening causes of acute chest pain in the 2021 AHA/ACC guideline~\citep{gulati2021chestpain} (acute coronary syndrome as NSTEMI/STEMI and unstable angina, pulmonary embolism, esophageal rupture as Boerhaave, and pneumothorax). Their union has seven conditions. Neither set involves a judgment of these vignettes, and both were fixed before the analysis.
On average the result is stronger than with DDXPlus's labels. Zero-shot, post-trained lists name 9--24 points more of the warranted union conditions in seven of eight settings (OLMo~3.1 32B $-0.3$, n.s.), and with worked examples 7--22 points more for the three Qwen models and OLMo~3 7B (OLMo~3.1 32B $+6.5$ and Mistral $+4.0$, n.s.); the harm-based and chest-pain sets give the same zero-shot pattern. The losses of specific conditions, however, are confined to OLMo, Mistral and the few-shot Qwen2.5 models. No Qwen model names any union condition significantly less often zero-shot, while OLMo~3 7B loses NSTEMI/STEMI and unstable angina at both temperatures (and pulmonary neoplasm at $T{=}1$), OLMo~3.1 32B loses NSTEMI/STEMI, pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax, and with worked examples Mistral loses four of the seven (pulmonary embolism 31 points), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct two and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct one (Boerhaave). When the true pathology is itself in the union set (140 cases), zero-shot post-trained lists contain it among their top five 10--26 points more often for four of five pairs (OLMo~3 7B $+9.9$, n.s.). Scored against the union set, the must-not-miss prompt names 15--26 points more of the warranted conditions than the standard prompt and 8--20 points more than two combined standard lists, a larger share of its gain than under DDXPlus's labels, at a cost of 0.7--1.5 more unwarranted union conditions per list.

\subsection{Chance-corrected pass@32 and other models' views}\label{sec:chance}
\paragraph{Chance.} With 49 listed conditions, part of pass@32 comes from answers that do not depend on the patient. We therefore also score each case's samples against the true pathology of a random case with a different pathology (Table~\ref{tab:chance}). Base models' samples then still reach 0.05--0.19 at pass@32 and post-trained ones 0.01--0.04, far below the 0.48 of a uniform guesser, because both concentrate on conditions that fit the presentation. Subtracting these values shrinks the loss: with each model at its best prompt it is 5.9--17.6 points, significant in four of six pairs (not for Qwen3-8B, 7.7, or Mistral, 5.9); with the same reference examples for both, 7.2--17.6 points (Qwen3-8B n.s.); with another model's examples, 4.9--14.8 (Qwen3-8B and Mistral n.s.). Zero-shot, the corrected loss is 7.6 points for Qwen3-8B, 3.6 (n.s.) for Qwen2.5-7B and 23.7 for OLMo~3 7B, and it disappears at 32B (0.7 and $-0.4$ points, n.s.). For Qwen2.5-72B, added later, the corrected loss is 8.8 points at the best prompt (significant) and $-0.9$ zero-shot (n.s.).

\paragraph{Other models' views.} The packing test of Table~\ref{tab:packing} compares a post-trained list with its base model's mean for the same patient against the base model's means for other patients with the same diagnosis, a lenient baseline that any list responding to the patient passes. Against other families' base models alone, every zero-shot post-trained list is closer to its own base model's mean ($-0.031$ to $-0.138$). Table~\ref{tab:packstrict} compares it with every other final model's mean for the same patient. For Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-32B and OLMo~3.1 32B the post-trained list is closer to its own base model's view than to any other base model's (by 0.036--0.058) and far closer than to the average post-trained model's (0.067--0.090), but about as close to the nearest other post-trained model's (n.s.). Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is as close to Qwen3-8B-Base's view as to its own base model's, and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct is closer to Qwen3-8B-Base's and Qwen3-8B's. For the stronger models, then, a post-trained list stays close to its own base model's view, while the stronger post-trained models also converge on one another.

\subsection{Ties, list size, validity, prevalence and the reference ceiling}\label{sec:further}
These checks use the zero-shot $T{=}0.7$ final pairs.
\emph{Ties.} Post-trained models' 32 samples are unanimous in 34--57\% of cases (Qwen3-8B 78\%), where agreement cannot rank anything. On the remaining cases agreement's AUROC is 0.61--0.66 for the post-trained models against 0.78--0.83 for their base models, so agreement weakens even where it is not tied. On those cases Qwen3-8B's stated probability no longer beats agreement (0.611 against 0.617): its advantage comes from cases where all samples agree, whereas OLMo-3-7B-Instruct's stated probability stays ahead (0.729 against 0.605).
\emph{List size.} The three most frequent of 32 samples can be fewer than three answers. With $m = \min(3, \text{distinct sampled answers})$, the first $m$ items of one list contain the true pathology about as often as the $m$ most frequent samples for the post-trained models ($-0.5$ to $-5.2$ points; significantly lower for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct), while for base models the samples win by 8.5--14.6. The advantage of a post-trained list's top three is that it names three conditions where its samples offer fewer.
\emph{Validity.} Counting invalid samples as wrong (as everywhere in the paper) or scoring valid samples only leaves pass@32 unchanged and moves pass@1, mostly for OLMo~3 7B, whose single-answer gain is $+7.1$ points with invalid samples counted as wrong and $-3.5$ (n.s.) over valid samples only, weighted to the natural prevalence below.
\emph{Prevalence.} The test sample is class-balanced (20 cases per pathology). Reweighted to the pathology frequencies of the full DDXPlus test split (134,529 patients), post-training costs 4.9--31.5 points of pass@32 (all intervals exclude zero, including both 32B pairs), raises recall@5 by 10.3--17.7 points for the Qwen models and OLMo~3.1 32B ($-0.3$ for OLMo~3 7B) and lowers one list's TV by 0.047--0.069 (OLMo~3 7B $+0.031$).
\emph{Reference ceiling.} The reference's own top five contains the true pathology in 96.9\% of cases (97.3\% at natural prevalence), against 0.47--0.84 for one model list.
\emph{What replaces acute pulmonary edema.} On the 54 cases whose reference gives acute pulmonary edema at least 0.1, the conditions whose share of lists rises most after post-training are mostly other must-not-miss conditions (pulmonary embolism for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, $+0.29$ and $+0.52$; pneumonia and pulmonary embolism for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct; unstable angina, panic attack and NSTEMI/STEMI for Qwen3-8B), but atrial fibrillation and influenza for OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct, whose lists name acute pulmonary edema 0.25 less often.

\subsection{List concentration, dangerous misses, selective prediction and common cases}\label{sec:joint}
Table~\ref{tab:r13pairs} adds four checks computed with the same loader as the headline tables. \emph{Concentration.} A five-item list could not get shorter, but its probabilities could concentrate. Zero-shot, the entropy of one list changes by $-0.13$ to $+0.08$ nats for the Qwen models and OLMo~3.1 32B, and with worked examples it rises for them ($+0.05$ to $+0.25$); only OLMo-3-7B-Instruct ($-0.52$ zero-shot) and Mistral-Instruct ($-0.18$ with examples) state markedly more concentrated lists. \emph{Dangerous misses.} Per case, post-trained lists leave out a severe true pathology 9--18 points less often zero-shot and name none of the warranted severe conditions about 10 points less often (OLMo~3.1 32B $-2.2$, n.s.). \emph{Selective prediction.} Ranking cases by agreement gives the higher accuracy at 50\% coverage for every base model. After post-training the stated probability does better for Qwen3-8B and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct zero-shot and for every post-trained model with worked examples; the area under the risk--coverage curve gives the same ordering. \emph{Common cases.} On the cases where both models give at least 16 valid samples, pass@16 over valid samples falls by 3.4--30.5 points zero-shot (n.s.\ for Qwen2.5-32B) and distinct answers by 1.5--2.7, so the collapse does not come from invalid answers; and on the cases where neither model's samples are unanimous, agreement's AUROC falls in every zero-shot pair (0.72--0.77 $\rightarrow$ 0.61--0.67).
