\subsection{A third family: Mistral-7B v0.3}\label{sec:mistral}
We repeat the comparison with Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, a family also studied by \citet{jang2026cannotsample}. With the zero-shot prompt the base model does not answer: 52\% of its samples at $T{=}0.7$ and 76\% at $T{=}1$ are invalid (it continues the document instead), and its valid answers mostly repeat the first listed condition, so its single-call accuracy is 6\% and the zero-shot pair is not informative. With the few-shot prompt of \S\ref{sec:fewshot} the base model answers validly (0.4\% invalid), and the pair reproduces the other families (Table~\ref{tab:third}). Post-training raises pass@1 by 14.0 points and lowers pass@32 by 14.5, cuts distinct answers from 5.0 to 1.3 and Cov@32 by 0.138, and moves the samples away from the reference (TV $+0.058$). Voting gains the base model 5.6 points and the Instruct model 0.8; the three most frequent of 32 samples beat one list by 12.6 points for the base model, while for the Instruct model the list is ahead by 7.0; agreement is the better error signal for the base model (AUROC 0.826 against 0.671) and the stated probability for the Instruct model (0.747 against 0.613). The stated list improves modestly (TV $-0.036$ and DDF1 $+0.046$, surviving clustering and Holm correction over 42 tests; $-0.023$ with the true pathology removed, which does not), the smallest significant gain of the three families, and 11 of the 17 severe conditions are named less often (3 significantly). Mistral-Instruct also names 0.5 conditions per list that are not among the 49.

\subsection{Thinking mode}\label{sec:thinking}
Qwen3-8B can reason in a thinking block before it answers; the main runs turn this off. With thinking on (zero-shot prompt, $T{=}0.7$, up to 8,192 tokens; traces average about 1,500 tokens and all end before the limit), the same weights behave differently (Table~\ref{tab:third}). Accuracy rises at both ends: pass@1 is 0.671 against 0.559 without thinking, and pass@32 is 0.815, above the non-thinking model (0.607) and level with the base model (0.732 zero-shot, $+8.4$ $[1.7,15.4]$ points, not surviving Holm correction over 42 tests; 0.809 with worked examples). The samples are still narrow (1.76 distinct answers against 3.77 for the base model; Cov@32 0.283 against 0.323) but no farther from the reference than the base model's (TV 0.745 against 0.750). The stated list is the closest of any 7--8B model (TV 0.670, against 0.700 without thinking). The shift in error signals reverses: agreement across 31 samples is again the better signal (AUROC 0.732 against 0.638; difference 0.094 $[0.027,0.170]$), as for base models, and voting gains 1.5 points (n.s.). The narrowing of the samples and the advantage of the stated probability are therefore properties of answering directly, which a reasoning mode largely undoes, consistent with the chain-of-thought prompt of \S\ref{sec:robust}.

\subsection{Averaging stated lists across calls}\label{sec:aggregate}
Stated lists can be averaged across calls, as samples can be voted. For each case we average the first 5 or 32 valid stated lists, each renormalized over the conditions it names, and score the mean against the reference (Table~\ref{tab:aggregate}). Averaging helps base models far more than post-trained ones, whose lists vary little between calls (at $T{=}0.7$ with the zero-shot prompt, 32 averaged lists name 7.6--13.4 conditions, against 16.6--22.0 for base models). The mean of five base-model lists is about as close to the reference as one post-trained list (Qwen3-8B 0.699 against 0.700, Qwen2.5-7B 0.717 against 0.717, OLMo~3.1 32B 0.691 against 0.701). With five lists on both sides, the post-trained mean is closer for Qwen2.5-7B under both prompts ($-0.025$ and $-0.027$) and for Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3-8B under one prompt each, not significantly closer for OLMo~3.1 32B (zero-shot) and Mistral (few-shot), and farther for OLMo~3 7B and few-shot OLMo~3.1 32B. Averaged base lists also name severe conditions at least as often, and more often for OLMo~3.1 32B, OLMo~3 7B, Mistral and few-shot Qwen2.5-32B (by 0.06--0.14). One post-trained call thus gets about as close to the reference as several base calls; the packing test (Table~\ref{tab:packing}) shows that it is a stabilized version of the base model's view of the patient rather than its literal average, and, as for the open-ended questions of \citet{lake2025overton}, post-training adds little that averaged base lists lack (five post-trained lists beat five base lists in four of eleven settings). Qwen3-8B's thinking mode goes furthest: five of its lists beat five base-model lists by more than any direct-answer model's (TV $-0.049$) and name more severe conditions ($+0.129$). For a post-trained model answering directly, averaging five lists instead of reading one improves TV by only 0.005--0.025 at $T{=}0.7$ (up to 0.038 at $T{=}1$); it names 6--17 points more severe conditions, mostly by naming 1.4 to 3.6 more conditions. Five post-trained lists still cover 0.44--0.50 of the reference mass at $T{=}0.7$ (OLMo~3 7B 0.37) with six to eight conditions, about twice what their 32 samples cover (0.22--0.28) and as much as a uniform guesser naming about 24 conditions (0.47), so the coverage deficit of \S\ref{sec:collapse} is one of the sampled readout.

\subsection{Which signal to use: combination and held-out audit}\label{sec:audit}
Whether the stated probability or agreement across samples is the better error signal varies across models, so we ask what predicts it and whether a practitioner can tell. We pool 56 model--setting combinations scored on DDXPlus: the base/post-trained pairs at both temperatures and with three prompts, the OLMo stages, the 32B models, the medical models (including three fine-tuned from Llama-3.1-8B, HuatuoGPT-o1-8B, AlphaMed-8B and UltraMedical-8B, which appear only here), our GRPO runs, and the full-distribution prompt. They share weights, prompts and temperatures, so we treat the correlations below as descriptive.
The stated probability's advantage over five-sample agreement correlates with the \emph{single-answer rate}, the share of cases whose five samples all give the same top answer (Spearman 0.75), with the stated probability's own AUROC (0.82; the gap contains this term, so part of this is by construction), and negatively with the number of distinct answers ($-0.74$). The stated probability is the better signal for 19 of the 56. No single-answer threshold separates them: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct still favors agreement, while OLMo~3 7B's DPO and Instruct models favor their unusually informative stated probability.
With five-sample agreement, as in the audit below, combining the signals beats choosing between them; with agreement across all 31 further samples the advantage shrinks (post-trained combinations: agreement 0.742, rank average 0.761, $+0.019$ $[-0.007,0.040]$; logistic 0.772, $+0.030$ $[0.013,0.044]$), and for the 17 base combinations agreement alone (0.821) beats the rank average (0.780) and ties the logistic combination (0.827). The rest of this section uses five-sample agreement. Fitting a logistic model of correctness on the stated probability and five-sample agreement with 100 labeled cases, and evaluating on the other 880, gives a mean held-out AUROC of 0.753 for the 39 post-trained combinations (0.765 for all 56); averaging the two signals' ranks without fitting gives 0.746; picking the better single signal on the same 100 cases gives 0.720; always using agreement 0.695; always using the stated probability 0.671. The logistic combination beats the single-signal pick for 35 of the 39 post-trained combinations. This matches the general finding that hybrids of consistency and verbalized confidence beat either~\citep{xiong2024express}.
For choosing a single signal, the simplest rule, always using agreement, is right for 66\% of the combinations (54\% of the 39 post-trained ones) and loses 0.025 AUROC on average (0.032). An audit does better: choose the signal with the higher AUROC on 100 random labeled cases, using five samples per case, and evaluate the choice on the other 880. Over 500 draws per combination it picks the better held-out signal 86\% of the time (82\% for post-trained models) and loses 0.005 AUROC (0.007); with 50 cases, 82\% and 0.010; with 200, 90\% and 0.003. It is reliable when the two signals differ by more than 0.05 AUROC (96\% of draws, 39 combinations) and close to a coin flip when they differ by less than 0.02 (53\%, 5 combinations), where the choice matters least. The audit's main cost is gold labels for 100 cases from the target population, and we validate it only within DDXPlus.

\subsection{Medical post-training}\label{sec:medical}
Applied after instruction tuning, medical RL does not cost coverage. AlphaMed matches or beats its parent at every $k$ (Figure~\ref{fig:alphamed}): +3.9 points at $k{=}1$ ($[-0.5,+8.5]$, n.s.), widening to +8.4 at $k{=}32$ ($[+2.7,+14.8]$). It reaches at least one correct sample for 47 of 49 conditions, against 39 for its parent.
It does not restore breadth, though: distinct answers (1.87 vs.\ 1.82), entropy (0.28 vs.\ 0.30), and coverage (0.27 vs.\ 0.24) stay at the instruction-tuned level, far below the base model.
AlphaMed also names off-list conditions more often than its parent, a mild loss of instruction following.
By condition, AlphaMed slightly \emph{raises} consideration in every severity tier (+2.2 to +4.3 points, significant only for the mild tier; Table~\ref{tab:severity}). It still loses acute pulmonary edema (0.31 to 0.13), and it introduces an attractor of its own: spontaneous pneumothorax as the top answer in 10.3\% of samples, against 4.3\% for its parent and a reference rate of 1.0\%.
Medical post-training thus operates on an already collapsed distribution; the collapse comes from the general post-training stage.
The other two descendants go further (Table~\ref{tab:medical}). HuatuoGPT-o1 (SFT then PPO) and m1 (SFT distillation from a reasoning teacher) both \emph{widen} the differential relative to their parent: 2.49 and 3.29 distinct answers vs.\ 1.82, and coverage@32 of 0.31 and 0.33 vs.\ 0.24. Their pass@32 rises by 13.7 $[+8.1,+20.0]$ and 18.1 $[+10.4,+26.2]$ points. m1 gains almost nothing at $k{=}1$ (+0.9, interval includes zero), so its improvement lies entirely in breadth. Both reasoning-trained models are also less calibrated (ECE 0.16 and 0.20 vs.\ 0.11). In these three models, medical post-training on an instruction-tuned model does not add to the collapse, and reasoning distillation partially reverses it.

\paragraph{Medical RL from the base model.}
Alongside the instruct-initialized AlphaMed-7B, the AlphaMed authors released a companion checkpoint, AlphaMed-7B-base-rl, initialized from Qwen2.5-7B rather than Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (according to its configuration file). The paper~\citep{liu2025alphamed} describes only the instruct-initialized models: GRPO with a binary correctness reward on about 19k multiple-choice questions from MedQA and MedMCQA, with a 64-question by 8-sample batch for 300 steps. It does not document the base-initialized checkpoint, so we cannot rule out differences in data or hyperparameters, and we treat it as corroborating rather than controlled evidence.
It offers a third-party check on whether RL itself causes the collapse (Table~\ref{tab:medical}, lower block).
It does not. RL from the base model improves on the base at every $k$ ($+14.3$ $[+10.4,+18.5]$ points at $k{=}1$, $+9.5$ $[+5.0,+15.0]$ at $k{=}32$). It keeps 3.14 distinct answers, against 1.87 for the instruct-initialized AlphaMed.
Against that instruct-model AlphaMed, it is 2.1 $[-3.0,+7.3]$ points worse at $k{=}1$ (n.s.) and 10.8 $[+5.6,+16.5]$ points better at $k{=}32$.
Its severe-tier Considered@32 shows no detectable change relative to the base ($-0.7$ $[-5.7,+5.3]$ points), against $-12.4$ for instruction tuning and $-8.1$ for instruction tuning followed by AlphaMed's RL (Table~\ref{tab:severity}; all well below the chance levels of \S\ref{sec:collapse}).
RL from a base model also narrows less in OLMo's RL-Zero at $T{=}1$ and in our GRPO runs (\S\ref{sec:training}), but not uniformly: RL-Zero at $T{=}0.7$ loses about as much as SFT, and within OLMo~3 7B's instruct pipeline the RL stage after SFT and DPO is the largest single narrowing (\S\ref{sec:stages}).

\subsection{Rare disease: overconfidence without accuracy}\label{sec:rare}
On 1,401 Phenopacket Store cases covering 749 diseases, every 7--8B model is near the floor: $\passk{1}$ is 1.4--2.2\% and $\passk{32}$ 3.7--7.0\% for the Qwen-family models, and lower for OLMo~3 7B (2.5--4.5\%).
Stated confidence is not near the floor. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct states a mean top-1 probability of 0.51, and its RL-trained medical descendants state 0.67 (HuatuoGPT-o1) and 0.69 (AlphaMed), while their accuracy is about 2\%. ECE accordingly rises from 0.49 to 0.64--0.67; at this accuracy ECE mostly restates mean confidence, so we read it as a rise in confidence without a matching rise in accuracy.
The RL-trained medical models (AlphaMed; HuatuoGPT-o1 after SFT) thus state much higher confidence where they are least accurate. The effect also appears without instruction tuning: AlphaMed's base-initialized checkpoint is the most overconfident Qwen-family model (mean confidence 0.71, ECE 0.70, accuracy 1.7\%).
The medical descendants do gain a little accuracy: AlphaMed beats its parent at $k \le 16$ ($+0.6$ $[+0.1,+1.1]$ points at $k{=}1$; $+1.0$ $[+0.0,+2.0]$, $p{=}0.06$, at $k{=}32$), HuatuoGPT-o1 at $k \le 8$, and m1 at $k \ge 4$ ($+1.4$ $[+0.3,+2.6]$ at $k{=}32$; intervals resample the 749 diseases). These gains are an order of magnitude smaller than the rise in confidence.
m1, trained only with supervised reasoning traces (at its intended 8k-token budget), is the exception on calibration and diversity: it is the most diverse model (15.3 distinct answers per 32 samples, against 11.5 for the parent and 9.2 for HuatuoGPT-o1), and its confidence rises least (0.57).

General post-training reproduces the DDXPlus pattern on Qwen3. Qwen3-8B beats its base at $\passk{1}$ ($+0.7$ $[+0.3,+1.2]$) and trails it from $k{=}8$ on, by $-2.2$ $[-3.3,-1.2]$ points at $\passk{32}$ (a relative loss of 37\%), with half the distinct answers (6.4 vs.\ 13.4). For Qwen2.5 no pass@$k$ difference is significant.
Unlike medical RL, general post-training \emph{lowers} stated confidence here (0.61 to 0.46 for Qwen3, 0.61 to 0.51 for Qwen2.5), although base models also give invalid answers more often (8.5\% of Qwen3-8B-Base samples).
OLMo~3 does not share this: every stage of its pipeline states a mean confidence of 0.73--0.84 at about 1\% accuracy ($\passk{32}$ 2.5--4.5\%), and its SFT checkpoint is the most overconfident model we evaluate (confidence 0.84, ECE 0.83).
On the 500-case subset, our 8B GRPO runs (\S\ref{sec:training}) are indistinguishable from their base (all pass@$k$ differences within $\pm0.6$ points).

Accuracy depends strongly on when the source case report was published (Table~\ref{tab:era}). For every model in the table, $\passk{32}$ is 5--10\% on cases published up to 2022 ($n{=}901$), at most 1.7\% on 2023--24 cases ($n{=}348$), and 2.6--4.6\% on 2025+ cases ($n{=}152$). The pattern is not monotone, since 2025+ cases score above 2023--24 cases, so case mix also matters; the gap between older and recent cases is consistent with, but does not establish, memorization of older case reports.

\subsection{Published case reports}\label{sec:medcase}
MedCaseReasoning presentations stop before the authors' differential, so these cases test open-ended diagnosis from real presentations (prompts and grading in Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}). We sampled the four zero-shot Qwen and OLMo pairs; OLMo~3.1 32B was left out for cost and Mistral because its base model needs worked examples, which this dataset cannot supply without reference lists. The two judges agree on 97.6\% of 391,987 distinct names ($\kappa$ 0.77; with only 4.5--6.3\% of names accepted, most agreement is on rejections); Phi-4 accepts more names, and the strict grading leaves every direction unchanged. The authors' alternatives were extracted by a language model from the reports' reasoning notes; we drop the 148 of 3,168 that are only category words (``infection'', ``malignancy'', ``viral infection''), which leaves 886 cases with at least one and moves no coverage figure by more than 0.4 points. We checked the judges against silver labels from string matching. Both accept 99.9--100\% of the sampled top answers whose words match the final diagnosis's (10,346), and at most 3.1\% (Mistral-Small) and 5.2\% (Phi-4) of those sharing no content word with it (155,522), an upper bound on false positives because abbreviations and synonyms fall among them. For the primary and strict grading these rates differ between base and post-trained models by at most 0.5 points (all intervals include zero); Phi-4 alone accepts 1.2 points fewer unrelated names from Qwen3-8B than from its base. The alternatives judge maps 94--97\% of exact matches to the right item and 5--7\% of names unrelated to every item to some item. The 17--28\% of top answers between the two silver classes are not checked. For voting, agreement and distinct answers, top answers are grouped by their normalized text whether correct or not. Grouping paraphrases by Mondo concept instead (with the normalizer used for Phenopacket Store, which resolves 29\% of distinct top-answer names; the rest keep their text) lowers distinct answers by 11--16\% for every model, leaves every post-trained minus base difference in distinct answers significant and in the same direction, keeps voting gains at or below 3.2 points and raises agreement's AUROC by 0.01--0.04; after post-training the stated probability then remains significantly better than agreement only for Qwen3-8B ($+0.063$ $[0.001,0.128]$; Qwen2.5-32B $+0.020$, n.s.), and for Qwen3-8B-Base agreement becomes significantly better ($-0.077$ $[-0.144,-0.009]$). To bound per-case judge false positives, which could favor base models because they give more distinct names, we also discarded every judge acceptance whose name shares no content word with its target (the final diagnosis, or the authors' item it was matched to). Every model's scores fall slightly and base models' a little more (coverage of the alternatives by 32 samples: Qwen2.5-7B base $-4.9$ points, Instruct $-2.9$), so the post-trained losses in that coverage shrink from 8--14 to 7--13 points for the Qwen pairs and keep their direction, and Qwen2.5-32B's pass@32 loss becomes significant ($-3.7$).
Against the alternatives the authors wrote down, the stated/sampled split replicates (Table~\ref{tab:medcase}): post-trained samples cover 8--14 points fewer of them for the Qwen pairs ($-2.9$, n.s., for OLMo~3 7B), one list covers them as before (equivalent within 5 points in every pair, TOST at the 5\% level), and for Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-32B one list covers more of them than 32 samples, whereas base models' samples cover more than their lists (by 1.1--10.2 points, n.s.\ for Qwen2.5-32B). The consequences follow DDXPlus in direction but are smaller. Voting helps little for any model ($+1.6$ to $+2.7$ points for base models, $-0.7$ to $+3.0$ after post-training), partly because paraphrases of the same diagnosis count as different answers. After post-training the stated probability ranks correctness at least as well as agreement for Qwen3-8B ($+0.085$ $[0.022,0.148]$) and Qwen2.5-32B ($+0.062$ $[0.006,0.117]$), both non-inferior at a margin of 0.03 AUROC; for the other two the difference is not significant and non-inferiority is not shown, and it gives higher accuracy at 50\% coverage for all four post-trained models; for base models agreement is not significantly different or, for OLMo~3 7B, better ($-0.172$). OLMo-3-7B-Instruct gives more distinct answers than its base model (24.6 against 13.7 among valid samples), whose answers are valid only 67\% of the time. Accuracy does not differ between cases published up to 2022 and from 2023 (e.g.\ Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct pass@32 0.49 and 0.52); since both periods may precede the models' training cutoffs, this does not rule out memorization.

\subsection{Closed-set case reports}\label{sec:closedcase}
To check the case-report results without a judge model, we gave each presentation a list of ten candidates: the final diagnosis, the authors' alternatives (category-only entries removed; 2,935 in all) and, to fill the list, final diagnoses of other cases that share no content word with any listed candidate, in random order. Answers are matched to the candidates by name (Table~\ref{tab:closedcase}). The split replicates in all four pairs, more sharply than with open-ended answers: after post-training the 32 samples cover 22--27 points fewer of the authors' alternatives and pass@32 falls by 11.5--23.6 points, while one list contains the final diagnosis 4.1--7.5 points more often and covers 2.5--6.9 points more of the alternatives. Within each post-trained model one list covers 37--64 points more of the alternatives than all 32 samples together, against 11--34 points for base models. With ten candidates a five-item list names half of them, so list coverage is partly mechanical; the contrasts between models and between readouts are not. Agreement's AUROC falls in all four pairs; after post-training the stated probability is the better signal for Qwen3-8B ($+0.104$ $[0.068,0.140]$), agreement for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($-0.047$ $[-0.090,-0.002]$), and the two tie for the others. Voting changes accuracy by at most 4 points for any model.

\subsection{Stated and sampled readouts on real rare-disease cases}\label{sec:phenoreadouts}
Phenopacket Store cases are real, but they have no reference differential and accuracy is near the floor, so we can test only the consequences of \S\ref{sec:consequences}, and we count an answer as correct if it is the diagnosis or a closely related Mondo class (exact matches give only 8--31 correct single-call answers per model). Top answers are grouped by Mondo class for voting and agreement (Table~\ref{tab:pheno}).
The DDXPlus shifts reappear, but the top-three comparison does not flip as it does on DDXPlus. Majority voting over 32 samples helps the base models by 3.1--4.6 points but the final post-trained models by only 0.4--1.5 (Qwen3-8B $+0.4$, n.s.). Post-training weakens agreement as an error signal (Qwen3-8B 0.830 $\rightarrow$ 0.763, Qwen2.5-7B 0.845 $\rightarrow$ 0.745, OLMo~3 7B 0.814 $\rightarrow$ 0.726) and strengthens the stated probability (0.567 $\rightarrow$ 0.707, 0.598 $\rightarrow$ 0.717, 0.464 $\rightarrow$ 0.652). Agreement beats the stated probability by 0.25--0.35 AUROC for the base models and by only 0.03--0.07 for the post-trained ones, significantly only for Qwen3-8B ($-0.056$ $[-0.120,-0.002]$). On these open-ended cases the three most frequent of 32 sampled answers still contain a correct diagnosis more often than one list's top three, but the gap shrinks from 4.6--7.0 points for the base models to 2.7--3.6 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct and to a tie for Qwen3-8B ($+0.4$ $[-0.8,+1.8]$). The medical models behave like their post-trained parent, with agreement the better signal for all of them.

\section{Training without collapsing the samples}\label{sec:training}
\emph{Related rewards.} Closely related GRPO rewards computed from group answer counts have appeared since these experiments: a witness advantage that trains models to sample the distributions they state~\citep{arabi2026samplewhat}, and a batch bonus that penalizes repeated answers~\citep{song2025outcome}. Our group reward \texttt{gm} additionally needs a reference differential at training time, which real clinical data rarely provide; we do not compare against them, and we treat the results below as existence results.

The stated list survives post-training, but sampled diversity still matters: self-consistency and other sampling-based methods depend on it (\S\ref{sec:consequences}), and so does reinforcement learning itself, since GRPO learns nothing from a group whose samples agree.
Can reinforcement learning raise diagnostic accuracy without collapsing the sampled differential? We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on DDXPlus training patients (9,800 cases, 200 per condition; disjoint from the test split) and evaluate exactly as in \S\ref{sec:setup}.

\paragraph{Setup.}
We train LoRA adapters ($r{=}32$) with GRPO for 200 steps. Each step uses 16 prompts and 16 sampled completions per prompt, generated with vLLM on the same GPU.
A first sweep with a common aggressive configuration (learning rate $2{\times}10^{-5}$, no KL penalty, 8 samples per prompt, per-group reward standardization) was unstable. In three of seven runs, the policy collapsed to an input-independent answer: one condition for 88--100\% of all patients, with completions shrinking to about 25 tokens.
The starting policy is nearly deterministic (token entropy ${\approx}0.06$), so most GRPO groups have zero reward variance, and noisy updates drive the collapse.
We therefore use learning rate $5{\times}10^{-6}$, KL coefficient 0.04, no reward standardization (as in \citet{puri2026beyondmode}), and 16 samples per prompt. A monitor tracks the number of distinct top-1 answers per case within each batch. All runs in this configuration were stable.

\paragraph{Rewards.}
Every recipe includes a format reward: the answer must parse into a list of distinct conditions with valid probabilities.
\texttt{acc} is standard RLVR: 1 if the top-1 answer is the true pathology.
\texttt{dist} adds two per-sample distributional terms to \texttt{acc}: a Brier score of the stated distribution against the truth, and the overlap of the stated distribution with the reference differential.
Both are computed from a \emph{single} completion. They cannot see that the policy gives the same answer in every sample, which is exactly the collapse of \S\ref{sec:collapse}.
\texttt{gm} adds to \texttt{acc} a \emph{group-level} reward over the GRPO group of $n$ samples for a case. If sample $i$'s top-1 answer is $a$, and $k_a$ samples in the group give $a$,
\begin{equation}
r_i^{\mathrm{gm}} = \operatorname{clip}\!\big(n\,p_{\mathrm{ref}}(a) - (k_a - 1),\ 0,\ 1\big),
\end{equation}
where $p_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference differential. This is sample $i$'s marginal contribution to $n\sum_c \min(q_c, p_{\mathrm{ref}}(c))$, the overlap between the group's empirical answer distribution $q$ and the reference. An answer earns credit while its condition is under-represented relative to its reference mass, and none once it is over-represented.
In contrast to multi-answer rewards that score a set inside one completion~\citep{puri2026beyondmode}, \texttt{gm} acts on the distribution of \emph{sampled} answers, the quantity that collapses.
Because the group reward fires only when a group contains dissenting samples, we also test a boosted variant, \texttt{gm}$^{+}$: \texttt{gm} weight 3 and training temperature 1.2.
As baselines we adapt the multi-answer rewards of \citet{puri2026beyondmode} to our prompt. \textsc{Multi-RLVR} scores the share of listed conditions that belong to the reference differential, treated as a set of acceptable answers; \textsc{Multi-RLCR} adds their set-level Brier term on the per-answer probabilities. Both zero the reward for duplicate or invalid answers, as in the original, and use the same format reward, optimizer and settings as our recipes.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:training} reports means over two seeds; intervals bootstrap cases and do not include seed-to-seed variation. All our recipes raise top-1 accuracy by 8--10 points; the multi-answer baselines barely move it (below).
The per-sample recipes (\texttt{acc}, \texttt{dist}) slightly \emph{reduce} diversity relative to the starting model, the sharpening documented in \S\ref{sec:general}.
The group reward removes this. \texttt{gm} matches the starting model's diversity, and \texttt{gm}$^{+}$ exceeds it while also being the most accurate recipe.
Against \texttt{acc}, with paired bootstraps over cases averaged over seeds, \texttt{gm}$^{+}$ improves:
\begin{itemize}
\item pass@1 by $+1.6$ $[+1.0,+2.3]$ and pass@32 by $+1.7$ $[+1.0,+2.6]$ points;
\item distinct answers by $+0.10$ $[+0.07,+0.13]$ and entropy by $+0.034$ $[+0.022,+0.047]$;
\item coverage@32 by $+1.5$ $[+1.0,+2.1]$ points, and TV by $-0.014$ $[-0.019,-0.010]$.
\end{itemize}
Plain \texttt{gm} improves on \texttt{acc} in the same direction with smaller margins (e.g.\ pass@1 $+1.0$ $[+0.6,+1.6]$, entropy $+0.013$ $[+0.005,+0.021]$).
Diversity increases monotonically with group-reward pressure, with no accuracy cost.
The set-membership baselines of \citet{puri2026beyondmode} train stably (their reward rises from 0.27--0.31 to 0.32--0.35) but barely change sampled behavior. pass@1 rises by under 1 point over the untrained model, and diversity is unchanged. Against them, \texttt{gm}$^{+}$ is better on every metric, by $+8.9$ $[+7.4,+10.5]$ points at pass@1, $+0.07$ $[+0.03,+0.11]$ distinct answers and $+3.0$ $[+2.3,+3.8]$ points of coverage@32 (vs.\ \textsc{Multi-RLVR}; \textsc{Multi-RLCR} is similar).
What they do improve is the differential written \emph{inside} one completion: the reference mass covered by a single listed differential rises to 0.317 (\textsc{Multi-RLVR}), against 0.300 for \texttt{acc} and 0.309 for \texttt{gm}$^{+}$.
The two objectives are complementary: a set reward shapes the list a model writes, while the group reward shapes which answer it commits to across samples, which is what collapses under post-training.
The absolute effects are modest because the starting policy is already collapsed: there is little exploration for any reward to act on.
None of the recipes changes rare-disease accuracy or confidence on Phenopacket Store, where a 1.7B model is at the floor; the same holds at 8B (\S\ref{sec:rare}).
\paragraph{Starting from a diverse base model.}
The 1.7B experiment starts from an already collapsed instruct model. We therefore repeat the comparison from Qwen3-8B-Base, the diverse base model of \S\ref{sec:general}, with the same recipe and \texttt{acc} vs.\ \texttt{gm}. We compare against Qwen's own post-trained Qwen3-8B (Table~\ref{tab:training8b}; means of two seeds).
Both RL recipes reach nearly the official model's top-1 accuracy (0.537 and 0.539 vs.\ 0.558; \texttt{gm}: $-1.9$ $[-3.9,+0.1]$ points). They keep more than twice its diversity (2.7--2.9 vs.\ 1.27 distinct answers) and beat it by 15--16 points at pass@32 (\texttt{gm}: $+16.3$ $[+14.0,+18.8]$).
In this setting, then, the collapse produced by general post-training is not required for its top-1 accuracy (our runs train on in-distribution DDXPlus data, so this is an existence result, not a like-for-like comparison of recipes).
Both runs still narrow the base model somewhat, and the group reward narrows it less. At equal pass@1 ($+0.2$, n.s.), \texttt{gm} beats \texttt{acc} on distinct answers $+0.14$ $[+0.11,+0.17]$, entropy $+0.035$ $[+0.029,+0.041]$, coverage@32 $+1.1$ $[+0.8,+1.5]$ points, and pass@32 $+1.2$ $[+0.5,+1.9]$. Each seed reproduces the ordering. The severe tier tells the same story (Table~\ref{tab:severity}): official post-training removes 9.8 points of can't-miss consideration, \texttt{acc} 2.8, and \texttt{gm} 1.5 (not significant). Figure~\ref{fig:grpo8b} shows the pass@$k$ curves.

\section{Condition-clustered intervals and multiple comparisons}\label{app:clustered}
The 112 headline tests below (14 metrics fixed in advance, eight zero-shot settings) are the primary analysis; every control, stage, few-shot and per-condition analysis is secondary, corrected within its own family, and read as a check on them. DDXPlus has 20 test cases for each of 49 true pathologies, and effects can be specific to a condition, so cases are not independent. Table~\ref{tab:clustered} gives the headline base-vs-post differences with a bootstrap that resamples the 49 pathologies with all their cases (50,000 resamples for these headline tests, so that results near the threshold do not flip between runs; 10,000 elsewhere). Two-sided p-values use the add-one correction, $2(1+\min(n_{\le 0}, n_{\ge 0}))/(B+1)$, so the smallest attainable value lies below the strictest Holm threshold, $0.05/112$. Holm correction runs over the 112 tests (8 pairs $\times$ 14 metrics fixed in advance: pass@1, pass@32, distinct answers, coverage@32, sampled TV, list TV, mass named, severe named, list and sample TV without the true pathology, DDF1, unwarranted severe conditions named, and the two AUROCs; the table shows seven). The same procedure is applied separately to the few-shot pairs (70 tests), the Mistral and thinking-mode pairs (42) and the stage and medical comparisons (154). Not surviving correction among the headline tests shown, marked $\dagger$: list TV without the true pathology for Qwen3-8B at $T{=}0.7$; sampled TV for Qwen2.5-7B at $T{=}0.7$; sampled TV for Qwen2.5-7B at $T{=}1$; pass@32 for Qwen2.5-32B at $T{=}0.7$; list TV for OLMo~3 7B at $T{=}0.7$; DDF1 for OLMo~3 7B at $T{=}0.7$; agreement AUROC for OLMo~3 7B at $T{=}0.7$; list TV for OLMo~3 7B at $T{=}1$; list TV without the true pathology for OLMo~3 7B at $T{=}1$; agreement AUROC for OLMo~3 7B at $T{=}1$; pass@32 for OLMo~3.1 32B at $T{=}0.7$; sampled TV for OLMo~3.1 32B at $T{=}0.7$; agreement AUROC for OLMo~3.1 32B at $T{=}0.7$. OLMo~3 7B's list TV without the true pathology at $T{=}0.7$ survives as a significant \emph{increase}.

\paragraph{Pooled effects and equivalence.} Statements such as ``robust only for Qwen'' compare significance across pairs. Table~\ref{tab:meta} instead pools each difference across pairs with a joint bootstrap over the 49 pathologies, which keeps the correlation between pairs scored on the same cases, and tests whether Qwen differs from the other families. The sampled collapse, the stated-list gain in recall and the weaker agreement are significant when pooled in all three prompt settings; agreement's AUROC falls by 0.10 zero-shot and 0.18--0.19 with worked examples. The stated list gains more for Qwen than for the other families in TV, conditional TV and severe conditions named in every setting, and in recall zero-shot and with reference examples; the zero-shot pass@32 loss is smaller for Qwen (by 7.1 points), mostly because OLMo~3 7B loses 28; and agreement falls more for Qwen only with reference examples. For claims of no difference we use two one-sided tests with margins fixed in advance (5 points for accuracy and recall, 0.02 for TV, 0.03 for AUROC). Thinking mode's pass@32 is at least its base model's (90\% interval $[+2.6,+14.1]$ points), but the non-significant zero-shot pass@32 losses at 32B and OLMo~3 7B's recall change ($+1.5$, $[-2.9,+5.9]$) are inconclusive rather than equivalent to zero.

\section{Prompts, vignettes and grading}\label{app:prompts}
\sloppy
\paragraph{DDXPlus.} Each patient's coded evidence is rendered by a fixed template into a vignette of the patient's answers and relevant history; we fix known mistranslations in the English evidence descriptions. An example (test case with true pathology chronic rhinosinusitis; the reference differential gives viral pharyngitis 0.17, chronic rhinosinusitis 0.16, cluster headache 0.15, acute rhinosinusitis 0.14, bronchitis 0.14, URTI 0.12; cluster headache is implausible for this patient, a reminder that the reference is an engine's posterior rather than a clinician's differential):
\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily
A 13-year-old female presents for evaluation. Symptoms (patient answers): Do you have pain somewhere, related to your reason for consulting? Yes. Characterize your pain: burning. Do you feel pain somewhere? mouth, forehead, cheek(R), cheek(L), nose. How intense is the pain? (scale 0-10) 3. [\dots] Have you lost your sense of smell? Yes. Do you have nasal congestion or a clear runny nose? Yes. Do you have a cough? Yes. Relevant history and risk factors: Have you had a cold in the last 2 weeks? Yes. [\dots] Do you have polyps in your nose? Yes. [\dots]
\end{quote}
System prompt: \texttt{You are an experienced emergency and primary care physician.} The user turn is the vignette followed by: \texttt{Based on the patient's answers above, give your differential diagnosis. Choose ONLY from this list of possible conditions: [the 49 conditions, one per line]. List the 5 most likely conditions from the list, most likely first, with your probability that each is the correct diagnosis. Use the condition names exactly as written in the list. End your answer with a JSON array in exactly this format: [\{"diagnosis": "<name>", "probability": <number between 0 and 1>\}, ...]}. The full-distribution prompt (\S\ref{sec:fullprompt}) instead asks for a probability on every condition, summing to one, most likely first. The plain and CoT variants are described in \S\ref{sec:robust}. Base models receive the same chat-formatted prompt; OLMo base models use their SFT checkpoint's chat template.
\paragraph{Phenopacket Store.} The vignette lists the case's present and (up to ten) excluded HPO phenotypes with sex and age. System prompt: \texttt{You are an expert clinical geneticist and diagnostician.} Instructions: \texttt{List the 5 most likely specific diagnoses (use the specific disease or subtype name, e.g.\ 'Spastic paraplegia 7' rather than 'hereditary spastic paraplegia', when you can), most likely first, with your probability that each is the correct diagnosis}, followed by the same JSON format.
\paragraph{Grading open-ended names.} Each predicted name is mapped to Mondo by exact lookup against Mondo labels and synonyms (also trying any parenthesized abbreviation and the name without it), then by fuzzy matching (token-sort ratio $\geq 92$). It is \emph{exact} if it maps to the Mondo class of the case's OMIM diagnosis, and \emph{related} if it maps to a specific ancestor group of it (at most two is-a steps up, with at most 150 descendants) or to one of its subtypes; siblings sharing only a broad parent are wrong. The grader passes hand-written checks (e.g.\ ``Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7)'' is exact for SPG7, ``Hereditary spastic paraplegia'' is related, and Turner syndrome is wrong for Jacobsen syndrome), but we did not validate it against clinician grading, so errors at the scale of the 1--2 point effects we report on this dataset are possible.

\fussy
%=====================================================================
\section{Limitations}
DDXPlus is synthetic: its reference differential is the posterior of a rule-based engine, and the simulated pathology is not always ranked first in it (it is for ``more than 70\%'' of patients~\citep[\S3.5]{fansi2022ddxplus}), so we treat TV and coverage as distance to a \emph{reference} posterior rather than to clinical truth.
Base models more often give invalid answers. We count these as errors, which makes the large-$k$ losses conservative but inflates post-trained gains at small $k$; conditioning on valid samples removes a quarter to a third of the $T{=}1$ pass@1 gain (\S\ref{sec:robust}). A re-run of the five final pairs with three worked examples in every prompt nearly removes invalid answers and confirms the results except OLMo~3.1 32B's stated-list gain (\S\ref{sec:fewshot}); it uses one temperature and one set of example patients, with lists from the reference or from Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct. Sampled hotter, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct recovers much of its base model's pass@32 but Qwen3-8B does not (\S\ref{sec:controls}); the temperature control covers two 7--8B models.
Our base/post-trained comparisons cover two open families at 7--32B, plus Qwen2.5-72B on DDXPlus at $T{=}0.7$ and Mistral-7B with few-shot prompts only; prompt robustness of the sampled readout is tested on one pair, and the collapse at large $k$ largely disappears when the model is asked to reason first (\S\ref{sec:robust}) or uses its thinking mode (\S\ref{sec:thinking}). The OLMo base models give invalid answers on 27--47\% of samples, so their format-controlled comparisons are weaker than Qwen's (below 0.5\% with few-shot prompts). We evaluate one RL-Zero checkpoint, at 7B, trained with an LM-judge reward on chat prompts rather than a diagnosis reward, and the 32B models only at $T{=}0.7$.
Severity is DDXPlus's own label; two published must-not-miss lists mapped onto its 49 conditions give the same average result but locate the specific losses in OLMo and Mistral (\S\ref{sec:extmnm}).
Phenopacket cases are drawn from published literature and may be in pretraining data, which we partly address with era splits.
The stated readout renormalizes each list's probabilities over the conditions it names, and the single-call answer is a model's first valid sample. A full-distribution prompt gives the same picture (\S\ref{sec:fullprompt}), but other elicitations may differ. Which readout is the better error signal is model-dependent; the audit of \S\ref{sec:audit} makes it checkable with 100 labeled cases but does not remove the dependence, and we validate it only within DDXPlus. The test set is class-balanced (20 cases per condition), so accuracies do not reflect real prevalence, and the prompt lists all 49 conditions, so DDXPlus is a closed-set task.
The free-length, closed-set and seeded-pick checks cover subsets of the pairs (\S\ref{sec:freelen}, \S\ref{sec:closedcase}, \S\ref{sec:seeded}), and the case-report judges are checked only against string-match silver labels.
We do not evaluate clinical utility with clinicians.
